# Group-Specific Thresholds
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/group-specific-thresholds.html
Summary: Learn how post-processing picks a different score cutoff per group to satisfy demographic parity or equal opportunity without retraining. See the thresholds on Tenant Screening, how they compare with the benchmark's S4 row, and why using the group at decision time can be unlawful.

> *One cutoff for everyone looks neutral. When score distributions differ by group, it is not.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Group-specific thresholds** are a post-processing mitigation: keep the trained model exactly as it is, and choose a different score cutoff for each group so that a chosen fairness criterion holds on the final decisions.

## Why It Matters

Many fairness fixes require retraining. Post-processing does not. When you inherit a scoring model, cannot touch it, or do not own the training pipeline, the cutoff is the one dial left. It is also the cleanest place to see the trade-off in numbers, because only one parameter per group changes.

It matters in practice too: Hardt, Price and Srebro (2016) showed that for a given score, the cutoffs that achieve equalized odds or equal opportunity can be found from the data, and the method is what Fairlearn's `ThresholdOptimizer` implements for the benchmark's S4 strategy. Seeing the plain version first makes the library version legible.

## Core Concept: Move the Cutoff, Not the Model

A single threshold `t` gives each group a positive rate `P(score >= t | group)`. If one group's scores sit higher on average, the same `t` produces different rates. To equalize a criterion, pick `t_g` per group:

* **Demographic parity:** choose `t_g` so each group's positive rate matches a target (here, the advantaged group's rate).
* **Equal opportunity:** choose `t_g` so each group's true-positive rate matches.

Both are quantile lookups on the scores. The one honest rule: fit the thresholds on training scores, then apply them to the test set. Choosing a cutoff on the test set that you then report on is circular.

## Concrete Example: Tenant Screening

The [Tenant Screening](../Tenant%20Screening/) audit: positive means the model flags a person as likely to reoffend within three years, the disadvantaged group is Black applicants, logistic regression, core features only, benchmark split.

```
one threshold (0.5)                accuracy 0.639 | positive rate advantaged 0.612 disadvantaged 0.725 | parity gap +0.1139 | TPR gap +0.0837
group thresholds, parity           accuracy 0.639 | positive rate advantaged 0.612 disadvantaged 0.598 | parity gap -0.0138 | TPR gap -0.0256
  disadvantaged-group threshold: 0.565 (advantaged stays 0.500)
group thresholds, equal opportunity accuracy 0.640 | positive rate advantaged 0.612 disadvantaged 0.611 | parity gap -0.0002 | TPR gap -0.0133
  disadvantaged-group threshold: 0.558
```

One threshold flags Black applicants at 72.5% against 61.2% for White applicants: a parity gap of +0.1139 and a true-positive-rate gap of +0.0837. Giving the disadvantaged group a cutoff of 0.565 (the other stays at 0.500) brings the parity gap to -0.0138 at the same 0.639 accuracy. The equal-opportunity cutoff of 0.558 brings the true-positive-rate gap to -0.0133 and the parity gap to -0.0002.

The benchmark's S2 baseline in `results/` (the current results) is the same model: accuracy 0.639 and a gap of +0.1139. Its S4 `post_processing` row, Fairlearn's `ThresholdOptimizer`, has a gap of -0.0054 at 0.639 accuracy. The hand-written version lands in the same place.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/group-specific-thresholds.py`; that file is generated from the block below).

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from faircode.manifest import load_manifest
from faircode.benchmark import _load_dataset      # the loader the benchmark harness uses
from faircode.strategies import encode_features
from faircode.models import build_model

def load_audit(folder):
    manifest = load_manifest(f"{folder}/audit.yaml")
    df, y, masks = _load_dataset(manifest)        # masks[name] is 1 for the disadvantaged group
    columns = list(dict.fromkeys(manifest.core_features))   # S2 feature set: no protected columns, no proxies
    X = encode_features(df, columns)
    train, test = train_test_split(np.arange(len(df)), test_size=manifest.test_size,
                                   random_state=manifest.random_state, stratify=y)
    return manifest, X, y, {k: v.to_numpy() for k, v in masks.items()}, train, test

manifest, X, y, masks, train, test = load_audit("Tenant Screening")
s_tr, s_te = masks["race"][train], masks["race"][test]
y_tr, y_te = y.iloc[train].to_numpy(), y.iloc[test].to_numpy()
model = build_model("logistic_regression", manifest.random_state).fit(X.iloc[train], y_tr)
p_tr, p_te = model.predict_proba(X.iloc[train])[:, 1], model.predict_proba(X.iloc[test])[:, 1]

def report(pred, name):
    tpr = [pred[(s_te == g) & (y_te == 1)].mean() for g in (0, 1)]
    print(f"{name:34s} accuracy {(pred == y_te).mean():.3f} | positive rate advantaged {pred[s_te == 0].mean():.3f} "
          f"disadvantaged {pred[s_te == 1].mean():.3f} | parity gap {pred[s_te == 1].mean() - pred[s_te == 0].mean():+.4f} "
          f"| TPR gap {tpr[1] - tpr[0]:+.4f}")

report((p_te >= 0.5).astype(int), "one threshold (0.5)")

# Demographic parity: give the disadvantaged group the threshold that matches the advantaged group's positive rate.
# Fit the threshold on the TRAINING scores only, then apply it to the test set.
target_rate = (p_tr[s_tr == 0] >= 0.5).mean()
t_dp = np.quantile(p_tr[s_tr == 1], 1 - target_rate)
report(np.where(s_te == 1, p_te >= t_dp, p_te >= 0.5).astype(int), "group thresholds, parity")
print(f"  disadvantaged-group threshold: {t_dp:.3f} (advantaged stays 0.500)")

# Equal opportunity: match the true-positive rate instead.
target_tpr = (p_tr[(s_tr == 0) & (y_tr == 1)] >= 0.5).mean()
t_eo = np.quantile(p_tr[(s_tr == 1) & (y_tr == 1)], 1 - target_tpr)
report(np.where(s_te == 1, p_te >= t_eo, p_te >= 0.5).astype(int), "group thresholds, equal opportunity")
print(f"  disadvantaged-group threshold: {t_eo:.3f}")
```

## Limitations

1. **It uses the group at decision time.** The final rule treats two applicants with the same score differently because of their group. In US employment, race-norming of test scores has been prohibited since the Civil Rights Act of 1991, and similar disparate-treatment rules apply in lending and housing. Check the law before using it.
2. **It needs the protected attribute at inference.** Many deployed systems do not have it, or are not allowed to use it.
3. **It breaks score calibration across groups.** A score of 0.55 now means different things in each group. See [Calibration](calibration.md).
4. **It hides the cause.** The gap came from the model and its features. Moving the cutoff reports a fair-looking outcome and leaves the cause untouched.
5. **One pair of thresholds satisfies one criterion.** The parity cutoff left a true-positive-rate gap of -0.0256, and the equal-opportunity cutoff left a gap of -0.0133. In general the criteria conflict, see [Fairness Metric Conflicts](fairness-metric-conflicts.md).

## Related Concepts

* [Reject Option Classification](reject-option-classification.md) - another post-processing method, applied only near the cutoff
* [Equal Opportunity](equal-opportunity.md) - the criterion behind the second set of thresholds
* [Demographic Parity](demographic-parity.md) - the criterion behind the first set
* [Calibration](calibration.md) - what group-specific cutoffs give up
* [Mitigation Strategies](mitigation-strategies.md) - S4 in the benchmark
* [How Does Unequal Cost Change a Fairness Evaluation?](cost-sensitive-evaluation.md) - expected cost per group when errors are not equally costly

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Tenant Screening/`](../Tenant%20Screening/) - the audit used for the example above
* [`results/`](../results/) - the benchmark rows quoted for S2 and S4

## Further Reading

* [Hardt, M., Price, E., Srebro, N. (2016): Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.02413) - NeurIPS 2016; the post-processing method and its derivation.
* [Corbett-Davies, S., Goel, S. (2018): The Measure and Mismeasure of Fairness](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.00023) - a critique of fairness definitions, including the cost of group-specific thresholds.
* [Agarwal, A. et al. (2018): A Reductions Approach to Fair Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02453) - ICML 2018; the Fairlearn reductions that the benchmark's S3 strategy uses.

# Permutation Tests for Fairness Gaps
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/permutation-test-fairness-gaps.html
Summary: Learn how shuffling group labels turns a fairness gap into a p-value, and how the same 5-point gap on Benefits Denial is significant in 72% of 1,000-row audits and only 17% of 200-row ones. Includes a hand-written test checked against faircode.significance.

> *A fairness gap is a number. Whether it is a finding or a coincidence depends on how many people it was measured on.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

A **permutation test for a fairness gap** asks how often a gap this large would appear if group membership carried no information at all, by shuffling the group labels many times and counting.

## Why It Matters

An audit reports "the positive rate for women is 5.9% and for men 10.9%". Is that a real disparity or sampling noise? On a 6,500-row test set it is overwhelming. On the 200-row test set of a small audit, the same gap often is not, and reading either one without a test leads to the wrong call: ignoring a real gap, or acting on an accident.

Every row in `results/results_fairness.csv` carries a `p_value`, a bootstrap interval (`ci_low`, `ci_high`) and a `significant` flag for exactly this reason. This explainer shows how that p-value is produced.

## Core Concept: Shuffle the Labels

The null hypothesis is that group label is irrelevant. If so, every assignment of "group A" and "group B" to the same rows was equally likely. So:

1. Compute the observed gap in positive rate.
2. Pool the predictions from both groups.
3. Shuffle the group labels, split, and recompute the gap. Repeat thousands of times.
4. The p-value is the share of shuffled gaps at least as large (in absolute value) as the observed one.

It is distribution-free and valid on the small, unbalanced groups audits keep running into. It complements the [bootstrap interval](bootstrap-confidence-intervals.md), which says how large the gap might be, while the permutation p-value says how surprising it is under no effect.

## Concrete Example: Benefits Denial

The [Benefits Denial](../Benefits%20Denial/) audit, logistic regression on core features, benchmark split. The model flags 5.9% of women and 10.9% of men as ineligible, a gap of -0.0509. First the full test set, with a hand-written test checked against `faircode.significance`. Then the same model and the same gap, audited on random subsamples of 200 and 1,000 rows.

```
test rows 6513: 2153 women, 4360 men | positive rate 0.059 vs 0.109 | gap -0.0509
hand-written p: 0.0 | faircode.significance p: 0.0
  200 rows: p < 0.05 in 17% of 200 random samples (median p 0.273)
 1000 rows: p < 0.05 in 72% of 200 random samples (median p 0.013)
```

On the full test set the p-value is below 1/2000 (the resolution of 2,000 shuffles), and the interval is -0.064 to -0.037. On 1,000 rows, a 5-point gap clears p < 0.05 in only 72% of samples. On 200 rows it clears it in only 17%. The gap did not change; the evidence did. The benchmark's German Credit S2 row has a gap of -0.0914 with a p-value of 0.17 in `results/` (the current results): a bigger gap than here, measured on about 200 test rows, and not significant.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/permutation-test-fairness-gaps.py`; that file is generated from the block below).

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from faircode.manifest import load_manifest
from faircode.benchmark import _load_dataset      # the loader the benchmark harness uses
from faircode.strategies import encode_features
from faircode.models import build_model

def load_audit(folder):
    manifest = load_manifest(f"{folder}/audit.yaml")
    df, y, masks = _load_dataset(manifest)        # masks[name] is 1 for the disadvantaged group
    columns = list(dict.fromkeys(manifest.core_features))   # S2 feature set: no protected columns, no proxies
    X = encode_features(df, columns)
    train, test = train_test_split(np.arange(len(df)), test_size=manifest.test_size,
                                   random_state=manifest.random_state, stratify=y)
    return manifest, X, y, {k: v.to_numpy() for k, v in masks.items()}, train, test
from faircode.significance import permutation_test

manifest, X, y, masks, train, test = load_audit("Benefits Denial")
sex = masks["sex"][test]                            # 1 = female
model = build_model("logistic_regression", manifest.random_state).fit(X.iloc[train], y.iloc[train])
pred = model.predict(X.iloc[test]).astype(float)
women, men = pred[sex == 1], pred[sex == 0]
print(f"test rows {len(pred)}: {len(women)} women, {len(men)} men | positive rate {women.mean():.3f} vs {men.mean():.3f} | gap {women.mean() - men.mean():+.4f}")

def permutation_p(a, b, n_permutations=2000, seed=42):
    """Two-sided p: how often does a random relabelling give a gap at least this big?"""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pooled = np.concatenate([a, b])
    observed = abs(a.mean() - b.mean())
    hits = 0
    for _ in range(n_permutations):
        rng.shuffle(pooled)                          # the group label carries no information (the null)
        hits += abs(pooled[:len(a)].mean() - pooled[len(a):].mean()) >= observed
    return hits / n_permutations

print("hand-written p:", permutation_p(women, men), "| faircode.significance p:", permutation_test(women, men, n_permutations=2000))

# The same model and the same 5-point gap, audited on smaller and smaller samples.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for n in (200, 1000):
    p_values = []
    for i in range(200):
        pick = rng.choice(len(pred), n, replace=False)
        a, b = pred[pick][sex[pick] == 1], pred[pick][sex[pick] == 0]
        if min(len(a), len(b)) >= 5:
            p_values.append(permutation_test(a, b, n_permutations=300, random_state=i))
    p_values = np.array(p_values)
    print(f"{n:5d} rows: p < 0.05 in {np.mean(p_values < 0.05):.0%} of {len(p_values)} random samples (median p {np.median(p_values):.3f})")
```

`faircode.significance.significance_report` returns the gap, the bootstrap interval, the p-value and a `small_sample_warning` for a group under 30 rows in one call.

## Limitations

1. **A p-value is not an effect size.** With enough rows, a 0.2 point gap is "significant". Read it next to the gap and its interval.
2. **A p of 0 means smaller than 1/n_permutations.** Report "p < 0.0005", not zero.
3. **It tests one test split, not the model.** Retraining with a different seed moves the gap. The test does not capture that variance.
4. **Many gaps means many chances.** The benchmark reports dozens of metrics per audit. See [Multiple Comparisons](multiple-comparisons.md).
5. **Exchangeability is an assumption.** If rows are duplicated, clustered by household or correlated in time, shuffling labels over-states the evidence. Use a grouped permutation.

## Related Concepts

* [Bootstrap Confidence Intervals](bootstrap-confidence-intervals.md) - the size of the gap, the companion to this test
* [Multiple Comparisons](multiple-comparisons.md) - what to do when you run many of these
* [Demographic Parity](demographic-parity.md) - the gap being tested here
* [Sampling Bias](sampling-bias.md) - why the sample may not represent the population
* [Subgroup Fairness](subgroup-fairness.md) - small intersections make the power problem worse

* [`Benefits Denial/`](../Benefits%20Denial/) - the audit used for the example above
* [`German Credit Lending/`](../German%20Credit%20Lending/) - a small audit where the test matters most
* [`results/`](../results/) - every benchmark row has a `p_value`

## Further Reading

* Fisher, R. A. (1935). *The Design of Experiments.* Oliver and Boyd - the origin of the permutation test.
* Ernst, M. D. (2004). Permutation Methods: A Basis for Exact Inference. Statistical Science 19(4); a clear modern account of why and when it is exact.
* Efron, B., Tibshirani, R. (1993). An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman and Hall; the companion interval method.

# Adversarial Debiasing
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/adversarial-debiasing.html
Summary: Learn how a predictor and an adversary are trained together so the scores carry no usable group information. See it on Tenant Screening, where raising the adversarial weight cuts the parity gap from +0.1136 to +0.0296 for about one point of accuracy, and why a stronger reader can still find what a weak one cannot.

> *Train a predictor while a second model tries to read race off its output, and punish the predictor whenever the second model succeeds.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Adversarial debiasing** is an in-processing mitigation that trains a predictor together with an adversary that tries to recover the protected attribute from the predictor's output, and updates the predictor to fit the label while making the adversary fail.

## Why It Matters

The repo's in-processing strategy, S3, hands Fairlearn a fairness constraint and asks it to find the most accurate model that satisfies it. That needs the constraint written down in advance. Adversarial debiasing states the goal differently: the model's scores should carry no usable information about the protected attribute. If the adversary cannot tell which group a score came from, the scores cannot be producing group-dependent decisions.

It also generalizes. The adversary can read a score, a hidden layer or a whole representation, which is why the idea is the basis of many neural-network fairness methods.

## Core Concept: A Two-Player Game

There are two models.

```
predictor:  p = sigmoid(w . x + b)          trained to predict the label y
adversary:  a = sigmoid(u * z + c)          trained to predict the group s from the predictor's logit z
```

The adversary minimizes its own loss. The predictor minimizes its task loss minus `alpha` times the adversary's loss:

```
predictor step:   d(task loss) / dz   -   alpha * d(adversary loss) / dz
```

`alpha` is the single dial. At `alpha = 0` it is ordinary logistic regression. As `alpha` grows, the predictor is pushed harder to produce scores the adversary cannot use. For demographic parity the adversary sees only the score. For equalized odds Zhang, Lemoine and Mitchell also feed it the true label.

## Concrete Example: Tenant Screening

[Tenant Screening](../Tenant%20Screening/): the model flags an applicant as likely to reoffend within three years, the disadvantaged group is Black applicants, the features are the audit's core columns, and the split is the benchmark's. Everything is plain NumPy: a predictor and an adversary updated in turn by gradient descent.

```
alpha  0.0: accuracy 0.639 | parity gap +0.1136 | race recoverable from the score, AUC 0.598
alpha  0.5: accuracy 0.639 | parity gap +0.0927 | race recoverable from the score, AUC 0.580
alpha  1.0: accuracy 0.637 | parity gap +0.0739 | race recoverable from the score, AUC 0.566
alpha  2.0: accuracy 0.637 | parity gap +0.0469 | race recoverable from the score, AUC 0.547
alpha  4.0: accuracy 0.628 | parity gap +0.0296 | race recoverable from the score, AUC 0.529
```

The `alpha = 0` row is the benchmark's S2 baseline in `results/` (the current results): 0.639 accuracy and a parity gap of +0.1139 (this run: +0.1136, because it is trained by gradient descent rather than scikit-learn's solver). Raising `alpha` to 4.0 cuts the gap to +0.0296 for 1.1 points of accuracy, and the adversary's ability to recover race from the score falls from an AUC of 0.598 toward chance (0.5). For comparison, the benchmark's S3 row (Fairlearn's `ExponentiatedGradient`) has a gap of +0.0172 at 0.626 accuracy, and its S4 row (`ThresholdOptimizer`) has -0.0054 at 0.639.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/adversarial-debiasing.py`; that file is generated from the block below).

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness

data = load_audit("Tenant Screening")            # S2 feature set: core features, no protected columns
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
X = data.X.to_numpy(dtype=float)
mean, std = X[train].mean(axis=0), X[train].std(axis=0) + 1e-9
X = (X - mean) / std
y = data.y.to_numpy(dtype=float)
s = data.masks["race"].to_numpy(dtype=float)      # 1 = Black applicants, the disadvantaged group
sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-np.clip(z, -30, 30)))

def train_predictor(alpha, steps=1500, lr=0.5):
    """Predictor p = sigmoid(X w + b). Adversary a = sigmoid(u * z + c) tries to read race from the
    predictor's own logit z. The predictor minimises task loss - alpha * adversary loss."""
    Xtr, ytr, str_ = X[train], y[train], s[train]
    w, b, u, c = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0.0, 0.1, 0.0
    for _ in range(steps):
        z = Xtr @ w + b
        p, a = sigmoid(z), sigmoid(u * z + c)
        # adversary step: get better at predicting race from z
        u -= lr * np.mean((a - str_) * z)
        c -= lr * np.mean(a - str_)
        # predictor step: fit the label, and push the adversary's loss UP
        dz = (p - ytr) - alpha * (a - str_) * u
        w -= lr * Xtr.T @ dz / len(ytr)
        b -= lr * dz.mean()
    return w, b

def report(alpha):
    w, b = train_predictor(alpha)
    z = X[test] @ w + b
    pred = (sigmoid(z) >= 0.5).astype(int)
    s_te, y_te = s[test], y[test]
    gap = pred[s_te == 1].mean() - pred[s_te == 0].mean()
    leak = roc_auc_score(s_te, z)                 # how well a threshold-free reader recovers race from the score
    print(f"alpha {alpha:4.1f}: accuracy {(pred == y_te).mean():.3f} | parity gap {gap:+.4f} | race recoverable from the score, AUC {leak:.3f}")

for alpha in (0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0):
    report(alpha)
```

The last column is the audit of the method itself: after training, a fresh reader tries to recover the attribute from the score. If its AUC is still high, the adversary lost.

## Limitations

1. **It is hard to train.** Two models chasing each other can oscillate. Step sizes, the number of steps and the initial adversary all matter, and a result at one setting says little about another.
2. **The adversary only removes what it can find.** Here it is a one-parameter logistic reader of the score. A stronger reader of the same score, or a reader of the inputs, may still find group information. Test with a different, stronger model.
3. **No guarantee for any single metric.** The gap fell steadily with `alpha`, but no `alpha` is "the one that satisfies parity". You pick a point on a curve.
4. **It costs accuracy, gradually.** 0.639 to 0.628 here, and the cost accelerates at larger `alpha`. See [Fairness-Accuracy Trade-off](fairness-accuracy-tradeoff.md).
5. **It needs the protected attribute during training**, even though the final model does not use it as an input.

## Related Concepts

* [Mitigation Strategies](mitigation-strategies.md) - where this sits among pre-, in- and post-processing
* [Fairness-Accuracy Trade-off](fairness-accuracy-tradeoff.md) - the cost curve every `alpha` traces
* [Fairness Through Unawareness](fairness-through-unawareness.md) - why not feeding the attribute in is not enough
* [Proxy Variables](proxy-variables.md) - the leakage the adversary is trying to find
* [Demographic Parity](demographic-parity.md) - the criterion the adversary above is built for

## Further Reading

* [Zhang, B. H., Lemoine, B., Mitchell, M. (2018): Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.07593) - AIES 2018; the predictor-adversary game and its gradient update.
* [Edwards, H., Storkey, A. (2016): Censoring Representations with an Adversary](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05897) - ICLR 2016; the earlier adversarial formulation for hiding an attribute.
* [Beutel, A. et al. (2017): Data Decisions and Theoretical Implications when Adversarially Learning Fair Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00075) - practical notes on what the adversary needs to see.

# Fairness Regularization
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/fairness-regularization.html
Summary: Learn how a penalty on the group gap is added to the training loss with one weight, and why a smooth gap on probabilities is not the gap on decisions. See the weight scan on Benefits Denial: nothing at small values, a closed gap at a cost of four points of accuracy at large ones.

> *Add the parity gap to the loss with a weight. The gap on probabilities is easy to shrink; the gap on decisions is the one that counts.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

A **fairness regularizer** is a penalty term for a fairness gap that is added to the training loss and weighted against accuracy by one number, so a single model fit trades the two off directly.

## Why It Matters

Constraint-based methods such as the benchmark's S3 (`ExponentiatedGradient`) enforce a gap limit. A regularizer is the soft version: no hard limit, just a price. That makes the trade-off visible as a curve you can read before choosing a point on it, and it works with any model you can train with gradients.

The catch is that decisions are thresholded, and a threshold is not differentiable. The penalty has to be written on something smooth, usually the predicted probabilities. A smooth gap and the real gap are different numbers, and the difference decides whether the method works.

## Core Concept: Loss Plus a Weighted Gap

```
total loss  =  log-loss  +  lambda * (soft gap)^2

soft gap    =  mean predicted probability for the disadvantaged group
               - mean predicted probability for the advantaged group
```

Squaring the gap makes it differentiable and treats a positive gap and a negative one alike. `lambda` is the price: at 0 you get the ordinary model, and as it grows the optimizer is willing to give up more accuracy to shrink the gap. The idea is the "prejudice remover" regularizer of Kamishima and colleagues, applied here to demographic parity.

## Concrete Example: Benefits Denial

[Benefits Denial](../Benefits%20Denial/): predicted above $50K income is the "ineligible" flag, women are the disadvantaged group, logistic regression on the audit's core features, the benchmark's split. Implemented with plain NumPy gradient descent.

```
  lambda  accuracy  soft gap  thresholded gap
       0     0.811   -0.0340          -0.0509
       1     0.811   -0.0332          -0.0516
      10     0.810   -0.0272          -0.0454
     100     0.794   -0.0090          -0.0212
    1000     0.770   +0.0043          +0.0010
   10000     0.759   +0.0013          +0.0000
```

The `lambda = 0` row is the benchmark's S2 baseline in `results/` (the current results): 0.811 accuracy and a thresholded gap of -0.0509. The in-processing strategy S3, a hard constraint, reaches -0.0219 at 0.784 accuracy.

Three things to read off the table:

- **Small penalties do nothing.** At `lambda = 1` the thresholded gap is -0.0516, no better than the baseline.
- **The two gaps differ.** At `lambda = 0` the soft gap is -0.0340 and the thresholded gap is -0.0509. The penalty shrinks the first one directly and the second one only through it.
- **Equalizing costs accuracy, and it accelerates.** The thresholded gap reaches +0.0010 at `lambda = 1000`, at 0.770 accuracy, 4.1 points below the baseline, and past that the gap does not move while accuracy keeps falling.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/fairness-regularization.py`; that file is generated from the block below).

```python
import numpy as np
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness

data = load_audit("Benefits Denial")             # S2 feature set: core features, no protected columns
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
X = data.X.to_numpy(dtype=float)
X = (X - X[train].mean(axis=0)) / (X[train].std(axis=0) + 1e-9)
y = data.y.to_numpy(dtype=float)
s = data.masks["sex"].to_numpy(dtype=float)      # 1 = women, the disadvantaged group
sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-np.clip(z, -30, 30)))

def fit(lam, steps=3000, lr=0.5):
    """Minimise  log-loss + lam * (soft parity gap)^2, where the soft gap is the difference in the
    group means of the predicted PROBABILITY (differentiable), not of the thresholded decision."""
    Xtr, ytr, str_ = X[train], y[train], s[train]
    w, b = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0.0
    g1, g0 = str_ == 1, str_ == 0
    for _ in range(steps):
        p = sigmoid(Xtr @ w + b)
        soft_gap = p[g1].mean() - p[g0].mean()
        dp = (p - ytr) / len(ytr)                                  # d log-loss / d z
        dgap = np.where(g1, 1 / g1.sum(), -1 / g0.sum()) * p * (1 - p)   # d soft_gap / d z
        dz = dp + lam * 2 * soft_gap * dgap
        w -= lr * Xtr.T @ dz
        b -= lr * dz.sum()
    return w, b

print(f"{'lambda':>8} {'accuracy':>9} {'soft gap':>9} {'thresholded gap':>16}")
for lam in (0, 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000):
    w, b = fit(lam)
    p = sigmoid(X[test] @ w + b)
    pred = (p >= 0.5).astype(int)
    s_te = s[test]
    print(f"{lam:8d} {(pred == y[test]).mean():9.3f} {p[s_te == 1].mean() - p[s_te == 0].mean():+9.4f} "
          f"{pred[s_te == 1].mean() - pred[s_te == 0].mean():+16.4f}")
```

## Limitations

1. **The penalty is a stand-in for the real gap.** The soft gap and the thresholded gap move together but are not the same, so always report the thresholded gap on held-out data.
2. **The useful range of `lambda` is narrow and data-dependent.** Little happens until about 10, the gap closes between 100 and 1000, and nothing further is gained after. Scan it on a log scale.
3. **It targets one metric.** This penalty is for demographic parity. Equalized odds needs a different term, and the two conflict, see [Fairness Metric Conflicts](fairness-metric-conflicts.md).
4. **It needs group labels while training.** The penalty is computed from group membership.
5. **You pick the point on the curve.** The method does not say which `lambda` is right. That is a policy choice about how much accuracy a smaller gap is worth.

## Related Concepts

* [Mitigation Strategies](mitigation-strategies.md) - S3 as a hard constraint, in contrast to this soft penalty
* [Fairness-Accuracy Trade-off](fairness-accuracy-tradeoff.md) - the curve this method draws
* [Demographic Parity](demographic-parity.md) - the gap being penalized
* [Fairness Metric Conflicts](fairness-metric-conflicts.md) - why one penalty cannot cover every metric
* [Adversarial Debiasing](adversarial-debiasing.md) - another soft, objective-level in-processing method

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Benefits Denial/`](../Benefits%20Denial/) - the audit used for the example above
* [`results/`](../results/) - the benchmark rows quoted for S2 and S3

## Further Reading

* Kamishima, T., Akaho, S., Asoh, H., Sakuma, J. (2012). Fairness-Aware Classifier with Prejudice Remover Regularizer. ECML PKDD - the regularizer approach to a discrimination-aware classifier.
* [Zafar, M. B. et al. (2017): Fairness Constraints: Mechanisms for Fair Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.05259) - AISTATS 2017; a covariance-based constraint that makes the same relaxation precise.
* [Agarwal, A. et al. (2018): A Reductions Approach to Fair Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.02453) - ICML 2018; the hard-constraint counterpart used by the benchmark's S3 strategy.

# Fair Representation Learning
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/fair-representation-learning.html
Summary: Learn how projecting out the directions that predict a protected attribute cleans a representation, and why the claim is only as strong as the reader you tested. See iterative nullspace projection on Benefits Denial: a linear reader drops to chance while a random forest still recovers sex at 0.859 AUC.

> *Hiding an attribute from one classifier is not the same as removing it. A representation can look clean to a linear reader and still be an open book to a forest.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Fair representation learning** transforms the inputs into a new representation that keeps the information needed for the task and drops the information about the protected attribute, so any model trained on the representation inherits the removal.

## Why It Matters

Dropping the protected column does not drop its information, because proxies carry it ([Proxy Variables](proxy-variables.md)). Fair representation learning attacks the proxies directly: it changes every row so the attribute cannot be read from what is left. Its attraction is separation of concerns. One team builds the cleaned representation, and downstream teams can train whatever model they like on it.

The risk is the word "cannot". It is only as strong as the reader you tested against, and that makes this the method where testing the claim matters most.

## Core Concept: Remove the Directions That Predict the Group

The simplest version is a linear projection. Fit a linear reader that predicts the group from the features, take its direction, and project every row onto the space orthogonal to it. Repeat on the result: the first projection removes the most obvious signal and the next reader finds what was left. This is iterative nullspace projection (Ravfogel and colleagues), and it is a linear-algebra cousin of the learned representations of Zemel and colleagues.

```
for k rounds:
    reader = linear model predicting the group from the current features
    remove the reader's direction from every row
```

After `k` rounds a linear reader can do no better than chance. Whether any reader can is the question the example answers.

## Concrete Example: Benefits Denial

[Benefits Denial](../Benefits%20Denial/): the features are the audit's core and proxy columns with the sex column removed (marital status, relationship, occupation and the rest, which do carry sex), standardized. The group is sex; the model is logistic regression on the cleaned rows.

```
columns: ['workclass', 'education', 'education.num', 'capital.gain', 'capital.loss', 'marital.status', 'occupation', 'relationship', 'hours.per.week', 'fnlwgt']
0 directions removed: accuracy 0.821 | parity gap -0.1336 | sex recoverable, AUC: linear reader 0.862, random forest 0.915
1 directions removed: accuracy 0.806 | parity gap -0.0480 | sex recoverable, AUC: linear reader 0.598, random forest 0.912
2 directions removed: accuracy 0.800 | parity gap -0.0259 | sex recoverable, AUC: linear reader 0.513, random forest 0.897
4 directions removed: accuracy 0.776 | parity gap -0.0070 | sex recoverable, AUC: linear reader 0.500, random forest 0.859
```

Two readers try to recover sex from each representation: a linear model, and a random forest that can find non-linear structure.

- **The linear reader is beaten quickly.** Its AUC falls from 0.862 to 0.598 after one direction and to 0.500 (chance) after four.
- **The random forest is not.** Its AUC is still 0.859 after four directions are removed, against 0.915 before. The group is still there; it is just no longer linearly separable.
- **The parity gap falls with it**, from -0.1336 to -0.0070, for 4.5 points of accuracy (0.821 to 0.776).

So the downstream logistic regression is nearly gap-free while the representation is not clean. The model benefits only because it is linear. A stronger downstream model could use what the forest finds.

The baseline here is standardized and fitted by scikit-learn on the S1 columns, so it is not the benchmark's S1 row (a gap of -0.1003 in `results/`, the current results).

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/fair-representation-learning.py`; that file is generated from the block below).

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness

data = load_audit("Benefits Denial", strategy="unawareness")   # core + proxy columns, no sex column
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
X = data.X.to_numpy(dtype=float)
X = (X - X[train].mean(axis=0)) / (X[train].std(axis=0) + 1e-9)
y = data.y.to_numpy()
s = data.masks["sex"].to_numpy()                  # 1 = women
print("columns:", list(data.X.columns))

def remove_directions(k):
    """Iterative nullspace projection: repeatedly fit a linear reader of sex on the training rows
    and project its direction out of every row."""
    P = np.eye(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(k):
        reader = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X[train] @ P, s[train])
        w = reader.coef_[0] @ P
        w = w / np.linalg.norm(w)
        P = (np.eye(len(w)) - np.outer(w, w)) @ P
    return X @ P

def report(k):
    Z = remove_directions(k)
    task = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(Z[train], y[train])
    pred = task.predict(Z[test])
    gap = pred[s[test] == 1].mean() - pred[s[test] == 0].mean()
    linear = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(Z[train], s[train])
    forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=data.random_state, n_jobs=-1).fit(Z[train], s[train])
    print(f"{k} directions removed: accuracy {(pred == y[test]).mean():.3f} | parity gap {gap:+.4f} | "
          f"sex recoverable, AUC: linear reader {roc_auc_score(s[test], linear.predict_proba(Z[test])[:, 1]):.3f}, "
          f"random forest {roc_auc_score(s[test], forest.predict_proba(Z[test])[:, 1]):.3f}")

for k in (0, 1, 2, 4):
    report(k)
```

The test of the claim is the last two numbers on each line: always try a reader stronger than the one you removed.

## Limitations

1. **"Removed" is relative to a reader.** A representation that hides the attribute from a linear model can still leak to a non-linear one, as the 0.859 random-forest AUC shows. Report the strongest reader you tried.
2. **It removes task signal too.** The directions that separate the groups are also directions that predict the label when the label itself is correlated with the group. Accuracy fell 4.5 points.
3. **It needs the attribute during training**, to fit the readers.
4. **It is fit on one dataset.** A new population has different correlations, and the projection no longer removes them. Refit and retest.
5. **It cleans the features, not the labels.** If the labels carry historical bias ([Label Bias](label-bias.md)), a model trained on clean features still learns it.

## Related Concepts

* [Proxy Variables](proxy-variables.md) - the signal the projection is removing
* [Fairness Through Unawareness](fairness-through-unawareness.md) - the starting point: dropping the column alone
* [Mitigation Strategies](mitigation-strategies.md) - the pre-processing family this belongs to
* [Adversarial Debiasing](adversarial-debiasing.md) - learns the removal instead of computing it
* [Label Bias](label-bias.md) - a bias a clean representation cannot fix

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Benefits Denial/`](../Benefits%20Denial/) - the audit used for the example above

## Further Reading

* [Zemel, R., Wu, Y., Swersky, K., Pitassi, T., Dwork, C. (2013): Learning Fair Representations](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/zemel13.html) - ICML 2013; the learned-representation formulation.
* [Ravfogel, S., Elazar, Y., Gonen, H., Twiton, M., Goldberg, Y. (2020): Null It Out: Guarding Protected Attributes by Iterative Nullspace Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07667) - ACL 2020; the projection method used above and its limits.
* [Edwards, H., Storkey, A. (2016): Censoring Representations with an Adversary](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05897) - ICLR 2016; learning the representation against an adversary instead.

# Measurement Bias
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/measurement-bias.html
Summary: Learn how a feature that is recorded differently for one group creates a gap the true values do not have. See injected mis-measurement on Benefits Denial: crediting women 15% less schooling doubles the parity gap while accuracy goes up, and noise instead of bias shrinks it.

> *A feature is a measurement, not the thing itself. When one group is measured worse than another, a gap appears that the true values do not contain.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Measurement bias** occurs when a feature or label is a noisier, or systematically different, measurement of the quantity you care about for one group than for another.

## Why It Matters

Arrest counts stand in for crime, cost stands in for health need ([The Obermeyer Case](obermeyer-cost-proxy.md)), a pulse oximeter reading stands in for blood oxygen. Each is a measurement, and measurements can be worse for some people: less care means fewer recorded diagnoses, a foreign degree may be credited at a lower level, an instrument may be calibrated on one skin tone.

A model trained on the measured values learns the measurement error as if it were signal. It is easy to confuse with two neighbours. [Label Bias](label-bias.md) is a biased target, a decision made by people. [Proxy Variables](proxy-variables.md) are real features that happen to correlate with a group. Measurement bias is a *distortion of a feature that is meant to be neutral*, and it is invisible in the data: the measured column looks fine.

## Core Concept: Systematic Error and Noise Are Different Problems

Two kinds of error behave differently:

1. **Systematic error (bias).** Every value for one group is shifted: recorded lower, rounded down, undercounted. The measured feature now separates the groups, and a model uses it to do so. The gap grows.
2. **Random error (noise).** Values for one group are scattered around the truth. The feature becomes less informative for that group, the model leans on it less for them, and the measured gap often *shrinks* while accuracy falls.

The first creates unfairness the true data does not contain. The second hides the true gap and degrades the group's predictions. Neither shows up as a missing value.

## Concrete Example: Benefits Denial

This is a simulation, because the real measurement process is not in the data: we inject mis-measurement into one column for women only and watch what changes. [Benefits Denial](../Benefits%20Denial/), logistic regression on the audit's core columns, the benchmark's split. The predicted-positive flag means "income above $50K, so ineligible".

```
true values                                    accuracy 0.811 | positive rate women 0.059 men 0.109 | parity gap -0.0509
education.num credited 15% low for women       accuracy 0.822 | positive rate women 0.040 men 0.149 | parity gap -0.1089
education.num noisy for women (sd 1.0x)        accuracy 0.799 | positive rate women 0.075 men 0.088 | parity gap -0.0135
capital.gain recorded 50% low for women        accuracy 0.812 | positive rate women 0.053 men 0.112 | parity gap -0.0592
```

- **True values:** accuracy 0.811 and a parity gap of -0.0509, the benchmark's S2 row in `results/` (the current results).
- **Crediting women 15% less schooling** (`education.num` scaled to 0.85) doubles the gap to -0.1089 and *raises* measured accuracy to 0.822. The error is systematic, so it encodes sex, and sex predicts the label in this data.
- **Noisy schooling for women** (noise with the column's own standard deviation) shrinks the gap to -0.0135 and lowers accuracy to 0.799. The model has stopped trusting the column, for women and for everyone.
- **Halving women's recorded capital gains** moves the gap only to -0.0592, because that column matters less to this model.

The point of the accuracy column: a model can look better on the recorded labels while it is worse for a group, because the labels never saw the true values.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/measurement-bias.py`; that file is generated from the block below). The function below applies a scale and/or noise to one column for one group.

```python
import numpy as np
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness
from faircode.models import build_model

data = load_audit("Benefits Denial")             # S2 feature set: core features, no protected columns
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
y_tr, y_te = data.y.iloc[train].to_numpy(), data.y.iloc[test].to_numpy()
women = data.masks["sex"].to_numpy()
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def measured(column, scale=1.0, noise=0.0):
    """Return the feature matrix as if `column` were mis-measured for women only: multiplied by
    `scale` (systematic under-recording) and/or with Gaussian noise (sd = noise * the column's sd)."""
    X = data.X.copy()
    col = X[column].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    bad = col * scale + rng.normal(0, noise * col.std(), len(col))
    X[column] = np.where(women == 1, bad, col)
    return X

def report(label, X):
    model = build_model("logistic_regression", data.random_state).fit(X.iloc[train], y_tr)
    pred = model.predict(X.iloc[test])
    w = women[test]
    print(f"{label:46s} accuracy {(pred == y_te).mean():.3f} | positive rate women {pred[w == 1].mean():.3f} "
          f"men {pred[w == 0].mean():.3f} | parity gap {pred[w == 1].mean() - pred[w == 0].mean():+.4f}")

report("true values", data.X)
report("education.num credited 15% low for women", measured("education.num", scale=0.85))
report("education.num noisy for women (sd 1.0x)", measured("education.num", noise=1.0))
report("capital.gain recorded 50% low for women", measured("capital.gain", scale=0.5))
```

To look for the real thing, compare the distribution of a feature by group for something that should be equal (for example, the same procedure code recorded at different rates), and check whether the feature's relationship to the outcome differs by group.

## Limitations

1. **The data does not show it.** You only see the measured column. You need an independent source of truth, or domain knowledge about how each group is measured, to know it is happening.
2. **The simulation is a guess about the error.** A 15% shift is illustrative. Real errors are not a clean scale or clean Gaussian noise, and they differ by feature.
3. **Higher accuracy is not reassurance.** Systematic error made accuracy go up here. Accuracy against the recorded label cannot detect it.
4. **Noise and bias point opposite ways.** Because noise shrinks the gap, a small measured gap is not proof of a small true gap.
5. **Fixing the model does not fix the measurement.** Mitigations act on the model; the repair is in how the quantity is recorded, or in choosing a different quantity.

## Related Concepts

* [Label Bias](label-bias.md) - when the target, not a feature, is distorted
* [Proxy Variables](proxy-variables.md) - real features that correlate with a group, as opposed to distorted ones
* [The Obermeyer Case](obermeyer-cost-proxy.md) - cost as a mis-measurement of health need
* [Missing Data as Bias in EHRs](missing-data-bias-ehr.md) - unequal access to care showing up as unequal records
* [Race Correction in Clinical Algorithms](race-correction-clinical-algorithms.md) - a measurement adjustment with its own fairness cost

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Benefits Denial/`](../Benefits%20Denial/) - the audit used for the simulation
* [`results/`](../results/) - the benchmark row quoted for S2

## Further Reading

* [Suresh, H., Guttag, J. (2021): A Framework for Understanding Sources of Harm throughout the Machine Learning Life Cycle](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.10002) - EAAMO 2021; places measurement bias among the other sources of harm.
* [Jacobs, A. Z., Wallach, H. (2021): Measurement and Fairness](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.05511) - FAccT 2021; treats fairness problems as mismatches between a construct and its measurement.
* [Obermeyer, Z. et al. (2019): Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aax2342) - Science 366; the well-known case of a cost measurement standing in for need.

# Aggregation Bias
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/aggregation-bias.html
Summary: Learn why a pooled model can fit every group worse than a model fitted to that group alone, and when separate models are not allowed. See COMPAS: separate models lift accuracy by 11 points for White defendants and 5.6 for Black defendants, with a coefficient that flips sign.

> *One model for everyone assumes the same features mean the same thing for everyone. When they do not, the pooled model is wrong for each group in a different way.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Aggregation bias** occurs when a single model is fitted to data from groups whose relationship between features and outcome differs, so the pooled model fits each group worse than a model fitted to that group alone.

## Why It Matters

A pooled model learns the average relationship. When the groups differ, the average is the right answer for nobody, and the group with less data is fitted the worst because it counts for less in the average. Medicine has long examples: the same lab value can mean different things by sex or ancestry, and a model fitted to the majority can be least accurate for the minority.

It is also the mirror of [Simpson's Paradox](simpsons-paradox.md) and of [Subgroup Fairness](subgroup-fairness.md): a trend in the aggregate that is not the trend inside each group.

## Core Concept: Pooled Versus Separate Models

The check is cheap. Fit one model on everyone and one model per group, and compare on each group's own test rows:

```
pooled model on group g's test rows      vs      model fitted on group g's training rows only
```

If the separate models are clearly better for a group, the relationship differs by group and a single set of coefficients cannot express both. Comparing the coefficients shows how: a coefficient that is positive in one group and negative in the other is the extreme case.

## Concrete Example: COMPAS

[COMPAS](../COMPAS/): the target is whether the COMPAS risk text is High or Medium, the features are the audit's core and proxy columns with race left out, logistic regression, the benchmark's split. Groups are White and Black defendants.

```
accuracy on the test rows of each group
  White defendants  pooled model 0.569 | model fitted on that group only 0.680
  Black defendants  pooled model 0.575 | model fitted on that group only 0.631

coefficient per standard deviation: pooled | White defendants only | Black defendants only
  Sex_Code_Text   +0.03 | -0.12 | +0.12
  MaritalStatus   +0.53 | +0.45 | +0.54
  CustodyStatus   -0.11 | -0.05 | -0.05
```

Fitting each group separately lifts accuracy from 0.569 to 0.680 for White defendants (11.1 points) and from 0.575 to 0.631 for Black defendants (5.6 points). The coefficient on `Sex_Code_Text` is -0.12 in one group and +0.12 in the other, while the pooled model puts it near zero (+0.03): the average of two opposite effects.

Two cautions. This model has only three features, so its absolute accuracy is low whatever the grouping; the comparison is the point. And a separate model per race needs the race at prediction time, which brings the legal problems discussed in [Group-Specific Thresholds](group-specific-thresholds.md).

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/aggregation-bias.py`; that file is generated from the block below).

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness

data = load_audit("COMPAS", strategy="unawareness")   # core + proxy columns, no race column
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
X = data.X.to_numpy(dtype=float)
X = (X - X[train].mean(axis=0)) / (X[train].std(axis=0) + 1e-9)
y = data.y.to_numpy()                             # 1 = scored High or Medium
black = data.masks["race"].to_numpy()             # 1 = Black defendants
columns = list(data.X.columns)
names = {0: "White defendants", 1: "Black defendants"}

def fit(rows):
    return LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X[rows], y[rows])

pooled = fit(train)
separate = {g: fit(train[black[train] == g]) for g in (0, 1)}

print("accuracy on the test rows of each group")
for g in (0, 1):
    rows = test[black[test] == g]
    print(f"  {names[g]:17s} pooled model {pooled.score(X[rows], y[rows]):.3f} | model fitted on that group only {separate[g].score(X[rows], y[rows]):.3f}")

print("\ncoefficient per standard deviation: pooled | White defendants only | Black defendants only")
for i, col in enumerate(columns):
    print(f"  {col:15s} {pooled.coef_[0][i]:+.2f} | {separate[0].coef_[0][i]:+.2f} | {separate[1].coef_[0][i]:+.2f}")
```

Run it on any audit by changing the folder name and the attribute. On some audits there is little to find: on Healthcare Readmission the pooled and separate models score within a tenth of a point of each other, so one model is fine there.

## Limitations

1. **Separate models may not be allowed.** Using the group at decision time can be unlawful in hiring, lending and housing. Check before acting on the finding.
2. **Smaller groups get noisier models.** A group with a few hundred rows fitted alone can overfit, so the gain above is partly a larger-sample gain for the bigger group.
3. **It is a test, not a cure.** The finding tells you the relationship differs, not why. The cause may be a [measurement problem](measurement-bias.md) in one group.
4. **Interactions can do the same job.** A single model with group-by-feature interactions can capture the difference without a model per group, and may be easier to defend.
5. **Pooled can be the better choice.** If the groups really share the relationship, pooling gives more data per coefficient. The check exists to tell the cases apart.

## Related Concepts

* [Simpson's Paradox](simpsons-paradox.md) - an aggregate trend that reverses inside the groups
* [Subgroup Fairness](subgroup-fairness.md) - why group-level behaviour needs group-level checks
* [Measurement Bias](measurement-bias.md) - a common reason the relationship differs
* [Group-Specific Thresholds](group-specific-thresholds.md) - the legal limits of treating groups differently
* [Class Imbalance](class-imbalance.md) - why the smaller group counts for less in a pooled fit

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`COMPAS/`](../COMPAS/) - the audit used for the example above

## Further Reading

* [Suresh, H., Guttag, J. (2021): A Framework for Understanding Sources of Harm throughout the Machine Learning Life Cycle](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.10002) - EAAMO 2021; defines aggregation bias in the taxonomy of harms.
* [Buolamwini, J., Gebru, T. (2018): Gender Shades](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v81/buolamwini18a.html) - FAT* 2018; a single aggregate accuracy hiding large differences between intersectional groups.
* Pearl, J. (2014). Understanding Simpson's Paradox. The American Statistician 68(1) - the aggregation reversal and when to trust which level.

# Survivorship Bias
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/survivorship-bias.html
Summary: Learn how training on the people who passed a gate shrinks the effect of the feature that made the gate. See AI Fair Recruitment: restricting to candidates with a test score of 70 or more nearly doubles the hire rate and attenuates the score coefficient from 0.97 to 0.83.

> *The data you have is the data that got through. If a filter chose who you see, the relationships you measure are the relationships among the survivors.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Survivorship bias** occurs when your data contains only the people who passed an earlier filter, so what you learn about the whole population from it is distorted.

## Why It Matters

The classic case is Abraham Wald's aircraft: engineers wanted armour where the returning planes were hit, and Wald saw that the planes missing from the sample were the ones hit elsewhere. The same logic runs through hiring and lending. You see job performance only for the people who were hired, repayment only for the people who were approved, retention only for the people who stayed.

A model trained on survivors has never seen the rejected, and it is tested on survivors too, so the damage is invisible in its metrics. The effect is not on rare edge cases: if a score decided who got through, the feature behind that score will look less predictive in the survivors than it is in everyone.

## Core Concept: Range Restriction and Selection

When a gate keeps people with a high value of some feature, two things follow in the survivors:

1. **Range restriction.** The gate's feature varies less, so its apparent link to the outcome weakens.
2. **A changed base rate.** The outcome is more common among survivors than in the population, so rates, gaps and calibration are all measured against a different baseline.

[Selection Bias](selection-bias.md) is the general family. Survivorship is the case where the filter is an earlier stage of the same process, and [Reject Inference](reject-inference.md) is the lending-specific attempt to correct for it.

## Concrete Example: AI Fair Recruitment

[AI Fair Recruitment](../AI%20Fair%20Recruitment/): the data has the hiring decision for every candidate, so the full picture is available for comparison. We then impose a gate: only candidates with a technical test score of 70 or more "reach" the stage we pretend to have data on. Logistic regression on every feature, standardized.

```
candidates 115309, passed the test gate 34695 (30.1%)
hire rate, everyone 0.259 | survivors only 0.473
gender gap in hire rate (women minus men), everyone -0.0292 | survivors only -0.0354

coefficient (per standard deviation), fitted on everyone vs on survivors only
  Experience_Years       +0.01   +0.01
  Technical_Test_Score   +0.97   +0.83
  Age                    +0.00   -0.00
  Gender                 +0.10   +0.08
```

- **The base rate nearly doubles.** The hire rate is 0.259 for everyone and 0.473 among the 30.1% who pass the gate.
- **The gap widens slightly.** The women-minus-men hire-rate gap is -0.0292 for everyone and -0.0354 among survivors.
- **The gate's own feature looks weaker.** The coefficient on `Technical_Test_Score` falls from +0.97 to +0.83 in survivors, the range-restriction effect. The `Gender` coefficient moves from +0.10 to +0.08.

The size of the distortion depends on how hard the gate is. A gate that keeps one in three is already enough to move the base rate and the effect of the gating feature.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/survivorship-bias.py`; that file is generated from the block below). The audit has the outcome for everyone, so we can compare against it; with real survivorship data you cannot, and the check is to ask what the gate was and model it.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness

data = load_audit("AI Fair Recruitment", strategy="baseline")   # every feature, Gender included
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
X = data.X
X_std = ((X - X.iloc[train].mean()) / (X.iloc[train].std() + 1e-9)).to_numpy(dtype=float)
y = data.y.to_numpy()
women = data.masks["gender"].to_numpy()
screen = X["Technical_Test_Score"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
columns = list(X.columns)

# The earlier gate: only candidates with a technical test score of 70 or more reach the stage we have data on.
survivor = screen >= 70
print(f"candidates {len(y)}, passed the test gate {survivor.sum()} ({survivor.mean():.1%})")
print(f"hire rate, everyone {y.mean():.3f} | survivors only {y[survivor].mean():.3f}")
print(f"gender gap in hire rate (women minus men), everyone {y[women == 1].mean() - y[women == 0].mean():+.4f} | "
      f"survivors only {y[survivor & (women == 1)].mean() - y[survivor & (women == 0)].mean():+.4f}")

def coefficients(rows):
    return LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_std[rows], y[rows]).coef_[0]

everyone, kept = coefficients(train), coefficients(train[survivor[train]])
print("\ncoefficient (per standard deviation), fitted on everyone vs on survivors only")
for i, col in enumerate(columns):
    print(f"  {col:22s} {everyone[i]:+.2f}   {kept[i]:+.2f}")
```

## Limitations

1. **You usually cannot see the comparison.** Here the full data exists; in practice the rejected have no outcome. The first defence is knowing the gate and its rule.
2. **The gate here is a clean threshold.** Real gates mix scores, judgement and chance, so the shift in base rates and coefficients is harder to predict.
3. **It does not always produce a larger gap.** The gap moved slightly here, and the sign and size depend on how the gate relates to the group.
4. **Reweighting helps only if the gate depends on observed features.** If the selection also depends on something unrecorded, no adjustment recovers the population.
5. **Evaluation inherits it.** Testing on survivors tells you about survivors. See [Disaggregated Evaluation](disaggregated-evaluation.md) for reporting results by group.

## Related Concepts

* [Selection Bias](selection-bias.md) - the general family of filtered samples
* [Reject Inference](reject-inference.md) - estimating outcomes for the applicants a lender turned away
* [Sampling Bias](sampling-bias.md) - when the sample is not drawn from the population at all
* [Label Bias](label-bias.md) - when the decision that produced the label was itself biased
* [Feedback Loop Bias](feedback-loop-bias.md) - when the filter decides what the next model sees

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`AI Fair Recruitment/`](../AI%20Fair%20Recruitment/) - the audit used for the example above

## Further Reading

* Mangel, M., Samaniego, F. J. (1984). Abraham Wald's Work on Aircraft Survivability. Journal of the American Statistical Association 79(386) - the aircraft-armour analysis.
* Lakkaraju, H. et al. (2017). The Selective Labels Problem: Evaluating Algorithmic Predictions in the Presence of Unobservables. KDD - outcomes observed only for the people a decision-maker chose.
* [Suresh, H., Guttag, J. (2021): A Framework for Understanding Sources of Harm throughout the Machine Learning Life Cycle](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.10002) - EAAMO 2021; where selection fits among the sources of harm.

# Disaggregated Evaluation
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/disaggregated-evaluation.html
Summary: Learn how to report every metric per group and per intersection with an interval, and how fast the intervals widen as groups shrink. See Insurance Denial: a 0.644 overall accuracy, and 95% intervals that grow from 0.116 wide overall to 0.333 for the smallest intersection.

> *An overall accuracy is an average over people. It tells you nothing about who is in the tail.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Disaggregated evaluation** reports every performance metric separately for each group, and for each intersection of groups, with an interval, instead of one number for the whole population.

## Why It Matters

A model can have a good headline number and fail one group badly, because the groups it fails are small. The Gender Shades study made this concrete: commercial face classifiers with high overall accuracy had error rates for darker-skinned women many times those for lighter-skinned men. Every fairness metric in this repo is a comparison of per-group numbers, so the discipline underneath them is simply to look at the per-group numbers first.

It has a cost that is easy to miss: small groups give wide intervals. A reported difference between two groups of 33 and 73 people can be pure chance, and an apparent absence of a gap in a tiny group can be the same.

## Core Concept: Slice, Then Put an Interval on Every Slice

1. **Pick the slices.** The protected attributes one at a time, and the intersections of them ([Intersectional Bias](intersectional-bias.md), [Subgroup Fairness](subgroup-fairness.md)).
2. **Compute each metric per slice**, not just accuracy: error rates, selection rate, calibration.
3. **Attach an interval** to each, by bootstrap ([Bootstrap Confidence Intervals](bootstrap-confidence-intervals.md)), and state a minimum group size below which you only report the interval, not the point estimate.
4. **Compare slices to the whole, and to each other,** using the interval, not the gap alone ([Permutation Tests for Fairness Gaps](permutation-test-fairness-gaps.md)).

## Concrete Example: Insurance Denial

[Insurance Denial](../Insurance%20Denial/): logistic regression on the audit's core features, the benchmark's split (267 test rows), groups by age and gender and their four intersections. Each row has a bootstrap 95% interval from 2,000 resamples.

```
overall accuracy 0.644

everyone                     n= 267  accuracy 0.644  95% CI [0.584, 0.700]  width 0.116
age: advantaged              n= 161  accuracy 0.671  95% CI [0.596, 0.745]  width 0.149
age: disadvantaged           n= 106  accuracy 0.604  95% CI [0.509, 0.698]  width 0.189
gender: advantaged           n= 133  accuracy 0.602  95% CI [0.519, 0.684]  width 0.165
gender: disadvantaged        n= 134  accuracy 0.687  95% CI [0.604, 0.761]  width 0.157
age 0 x gender 0             n=  60  accuracy 0.633  95% CI [0.500, 0.750]  width 0.250
age 0 x gender 1             n= 101  accuracy 0.693  95% CI [0.604, 0.782]  width 0.178
age 1 x gender 0             n=  73  accuracy 0.575  95% CI [0.466, 0.699]  width 0.233
age 1 x gender 1             n=  33  accuracy 0.667  95% CI [0.485, 0.818]  width 0.333
```

The overall figure, 0.644 with an interval 0.116 wide, hides the spread: age-disadvantaged is 0.604 against 0.671 for the advantaged group, gender-disadvantaged is 0.687 against 0.602 for the advantaged. The intersections are more extreme in both directions, and their intervals are far wider: 0.250 for 60 people and 0.333 for 33. Every one of those intervals contains the overall accuracy, so this test set cannot establish a gap between any two of them. That is the lesson, not a failing of the method: with 267 rows the audit cannot say much about any intersection.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/disaggregated-evaluation.py`; that file is generated from the block below).

```python
import numpy as np
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness
from faircode.models import build_model

data = load_audit("Insurance Denial")            # S2 feature set; groups are age x gender
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
model = build_model("logistic_regression", data.random_state).fit(data.X.iloc[train], data.y.iloc[train])
pred = model.predict(data.X.iloc[test])
y_te = data.y.iloc[test].to_numpy()
older = data.masks["age"].to_numpy()[test]       # 1 = the disadvantaged age group
female = data.masks["gender"].to_numpy()[test]   # 1 = the disadvantaged gender group
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def row(label, mask):
    correct = (pred == y_te)[mask]
    boots = [rng.choice(correct, len(correct)).mean() for _ in range(2000)]
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
    print(f"{label:28s} n={mask.sum():4d}  accuracy {correct.mean():.3f}  95% CI [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]  width {hi - lo:.3f}")

print(f"overall accuracy {(pred == y_te).mean():.3f}\n")
row("everyone", np.ones(len(y_te), dtype=bool))
for a, an in ((0, "age: advantaged"), (1, "age: disadvantaged")):
    row(an, older == a)
for g, gn in ((0, "gender: advantaged"), (1, "gender: disadvantaged")):
    row(gn, female == g)
for a in (0, 1):
    for g in (0, 1):
        row(f"age {a} x gender {g}", (older == a) & (female == g))
```

## Limitations

1. **More slices mean more chances for an alarming number.** Twenty slices will throw up a bad-looking one by chance. See [Multiple Comparisons](multiple-comparisons.md).
2. **Small slices cannot be evaluated.** The honest output for a 33-row slice is "unknown, wide interval", and a minimum group size makes that rule explicit.
3. **Intersections explode.** Three attributes with four values each is 64 cells, and most will be too small to report.
4. **The slices must match the harm.** Slicing on a column that does not correspond to anyone's real group membership produces tidy tables and no insight.
5. **Per-group accuracy is one metric.** Equal accuracy can coexist with very different error types, see [Accuracy Equality](accuracy-equality.md) and [Treatment Equality](treatment-equality.md).

## Related Concepts

* [Subgroup Fairness](subgroup-fairness.md) - why group-level checks need group-level data
* [Intersectional Bias](intersectional-bias.md) - the slices that cross attributes
* [Bootstrap Confidence Intervals](bootstrap-confidence-intervals.md) - the interval on each slice
* [Permutation Tests for Fairness Gaps](permutation-test-fairness-gaps.md) - the test for a gap between two slices
* [Multiple Comparisons](multiple-comparisons.md) - what to do when you report many slices
* [What Is an AUC Gap Between Groups?](auc-gaps-by-group.md) - the same curve computed per group, with an interval for the gap

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Insurance Denial/`](../Insurance%20Denial/) - the audit used for the example above
* [Open Dataset Profiler](../profiler.html) - reports group sizes and warns on small groups before you model

## Further Reading

* [Barocas, S. et al. (2021): Designing Disaggregated Evaluations of AI Systems: Choices, Considerations, and Tradeoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.06076) - AIES 2021; the design decisions in a disaggregated evaluation.
* [Buolamwini, J., Gebru, T. (2018): Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v81/buolamwini18a.html) - FAT* 2018; the study that made per-group reporting standard.
* [Barocas, S., Hardt, M., Narayanan, A. (2023): Fairness and Machine Learning](https://fairmlbook.org) - MIT Press; the chapter on evaluation and the case for looking at group-level error.

# Leave-One-Group-Out Evaluation
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/leave-one-group-out-evaluation.html
Summary: Learn how holding out one group at a time tests generalization to people the training data left out. See Benefits Denial with a random forest: most held-out groups change by a point or less, one 67-row group loses 4.5, and the test sizes say which of those to trust.

> *Cross-validation asks whether the model works on new rows. Leave-one-group-out asks whether it works on new kinds of people.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Leave-one-group-out evaluation** trains the model with one group removed from the training data and tests it on that group, to measure how well it generalizes to people the training data never contained.

## Why It Matters

A random test split is drawn from the same population as the training data, so every group is represented in both. Real deployments are not so tidy: a model built in one region gets used in another, a model trained before a policy change meets applicants after it, a group that was rare in training turns out to be common in use.

Holding a group out simulates that. It is a close relative of the [distribution shifts](distribution-shift.md) that wreck models in production, and of the worst-group evaluations behind benchmarks like WILDS. It is also an honest check on a quiet assumption: that the groups you did see are enough to cover the groups you did not.

## Core Concept: Hold Out the Group, Not Random Rows

```
for each group g:
    train on everyone except g
    test on g, and compare with the model trained on everyone
```

The comparison that matters is the drop in accuracy on `g`: the cost of never having seen it. A large drop means the model leans on the group's presence. A drop near zero means either that other groups cover it, or that the model barely depends on whatever distinguishes it. The groups should be real axes of variation (a region, a site, a time period), not an arbitrary label.

## Concrete Example: Benefits Denial

[Benefits Denial](../Benefits%20Denial/): a random forest on every column of the audit (race and native country included, so the model can use the group), the benchmark's split, with each race and each of the four most common native countries held out in turn.

```
race (random_forest)
  held-out group       test rows  with it  without it   change
  Amer-Indian-Eskimo          67    0.910       0.866   -0.045
  Asian-Pac-Islander         196    0.847       0.837   -0.010
  Black                      579    0.924       0.927   +0.003
  Other                       44    0.955       0.955   +0.000
  White                     5627    0.843       0.837   -0.006

native.country (random_forest)
  held-out group       test rows  with it  without it   change
  ?                          136    0.875       0.868   -0.007
  Mexico                     144    0.944       0.938   -0.007
  Philippines                 30    0.800       0.767   -0.033
  United-States             5825    0.848       0.828   -0.020
```

For most groups, removing them from training changes accuracy on them by a point or less. The largest drops are 4.5 points for the 67 American Indian or Eskimo test rows, 3.3 points for the 30 Philippines rows, and 2.0 for United States, the largest group. The two largest drops are in groups of 67 and 30 rows, where one or two rows move accuracy by more than a point, so treat them as a prompt to check, not a result.

The overall reading: on this data a forest generalizes to a held-out group about as well as it does to a random sample. That is a finding worth stating, because it supports the assumption that groups seen cover groups unseen. On an audit whose groups differ more, it would not.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/leave-one-group-out-evaluation.py`; that file is generated from the block below).

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness
from faircode.models import build_model

data = load_audit("Benefits Denial", strategy="baseline")     # baseline: every feature, race and native.country included
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
X, y = data.X, data.y.to_numpy()

def leave_one_group_out(column, labels, model_name="random_forest", min_rows=30):
    """For each group: accuracy on its test rows from a model trained with everyone, and from a model
    trained on every group EXCEPT that one."""
    codes = data.X_all[column].to_numpy()
    everyone = build_model(model_name, data.random_state).fit(X.iloc[train], y[train])
    print(f"{column} ({model_name})")
    print(f"  {'held-out group':20s} {'test rows':>9} {'with it':>8} {'without it':>11} {'change':>8}")
    for code, label in labels.items():
        held = test[codes[test] == code]
        if len(held) < min_rows:
            continue
        kept = train[codes[train] != code]
        without = build_model(model_name, data.random_state).fit(X.iloc[kept], y[kept])
        a, b = everyone.score(X.iloc[held], y[held]), without.score(X.iloc[held], y[held])
        print(f"  {label:20s} {len(held):9d} {a:8.3f} {b:11.3f} {b - a:+8.3f}")

raw = pd.read_csv("Benefits Denial/adult.csv", usecols=["race", "native.country"])
race_names = dict(enumerate(sorted(raw["race"].unique())))          # the harness codes text columns alphabetically
leave_one_group_out("race", race_names)
print()
country_names = dict(enumerate(sorted(raw["native.country"].unique())))
common = raw["native.country"].value_counts().index[:4]
leave_one_group_out("native.country", {c: n for c, n in country_names.items() if n in set(common)})
```

Change the column and the label dictionary to hold out something else, such as a region or an age band.

## Limitations

1. **Small held-out groups are noisy.** A drop measured on 30 rows can be chance. Report the group size and an interval ([Bootstrap Confidence Intervals](bootstrap-confidence-intervals.md)).
2. **It measures dependence on the group, not unfairness.** A model can generalize perfectly and still be unfair to the group. It is a robustness check next to [Disaggregated Evaluation](disaggregated-evaluation.md), not a replacement.
3. **A simple model may not care.** When we held out whole age bands, weekly-hours bands and education levels from a logistic regression on the same data, accuracy on the held-out group changed by at most 1.4 points, because other groups covered the same feature values. The check is most informative for flexible models.
4. **The groups must be meaningful.** Holding out a random label tests nothing.
5. **It trains the model many times.** One fit per group, which is costly for large models.

## Related Concepts

* [Distribution Shift](distribution-shift.md) - the real-world version of an unseen group
* [Subgroup Fairness](subgroup-fairness.md) - why group-level behaviour needs group-level checks
* [Disaggregated Evaluation](disaggregated-evaluation.md) - the companion check on groups the model did see
* [Sampling Bias](sampling-bias.md) - when a group is missing from training by accident
* [Max-Min (Rawlsian) Fairness](maxmin-fairness.md) - an objective that targets the worst group

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Benefits Denial/`](../Benefits%20Denial/) - the audit used for the example above

## Further Reading

* [Koh, P. W. et al. (2021): WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.07421) - ICML 2021; benchmarks built around held-out groups and worst-group accuracy.
* [Sagawa, S., Koh, P. W., Hashimoto, T., Liang, P. (2020): Distributionally Robust Neural Networks for Group Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08731) - ICLR 2020; the worst-group objective that this evaluation motivates.
* Quinonero-Candela, J. et al. (eds.) (2009). Dataset Shift in Machine Learning. MIT Press - the standard reference on how and why test data differs from training data.
