# Choosing a Fairness Metric
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/choosing-a-fairness-metric.html
Summary: Learn a decision path from the harm you worry about to the metric that measures it. See the benchmark's own results: in 9 of 13 audit and attribute pairs some fairness metrics are significant and others are not, so the choice changes the verdict.

> *There is no best fairness metric. There is the metric that measures the harm you are trying to prevent, and the others that will disagree with it.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Choosing a fairness metric** is deciding which group-level comparison matches the harm at stake and the standard you are held to, before looking at any numbers.

## Why It Matters

The metrics in this repo answer different questions: [Demographic Parity](demographic-parity.md) asks whether groups are selected at the same rate, [Equal Opportunity](equal-opportunity.md) whether qualified people are accepted at the same rate, [Predictive Parity](predictive-parity.md) whether a positive means the same thing for everyone. They are not interchangeable and, outside special cases, they cannot all hold at once ([Fairness Metric Conflicts](fairness-metric-conflicts.md)).

That makes the choice consequential. Pick afterwards and you can find a metric that says what you hoped. The benchmark's own results show how often they diverge.

## Core Concept: Start From the Harm

Work backwards from what goes wrong for a person:

| The harm | Who it hits | The question | Start with |
|----------|-------------|--------------|------------|
| Not selected when you should have been | Qualified people in one group | Are qualified people accepted at the same rate? | [Equal Opportunity](equal-opportunity.md) |
| Wrongly flagged or denied | People who would have been fine | Are false flags equally common? | False positive rate, in [Equalized Odds](equalized-odds.md) |
| Unequal access to a benefit | Everyone in a group | Are groups selected at the same rate? | [Demographic Parity](demographic-parity.md) and [Disparate Impact](disparate-impact.md) |
| A score that means different things | People relying on the score | Does a positive predict the outcome equally? | [Predictive Parity](predictive-parity.md) and [Calibration](calibration.md) |
| One group is simply worse served | The worst-off group | How well off is the worst group? | [Max-Min (Rawlsian) Fairness](maxmin-fairness.md) |

Then check the standard you are held to (a legal threshold such as the 80% rule, a regulator's named metric), and what the label means: if the label is itself biased ([Label Bias](label-bias.md)), the error-rate metrics inherit it and demographic parity may be the safer reading.

## Concrete Example: The Benchmark's Own Results

For every audit and protected attribute, take the benchmark's S2 model (logistic regression, no protected column, no proxies) in `results/` (the current results) and list which of the six metrics are significant. If the metrics agreed, each row would be all or nothing.

```
audit                    attribute        flagged  which metrics are significant
ai_fair_recruitment      gender           1/6     accuracy_equality
benefits_denial          age              3/6     accuracy_equality, demographic_parity, disparate_impact_ratio
benefits_denial          national_origin  1/6     accuracy_equality
benefits_denial          race             3/6     accuracy_equality, demographic_parity, disparate_impact_ratio
benefits_denial          sex              4/6     accuracy_equality, demographic_parity, disparate_impact_ratio, predictive_parity
compas                   race             6/6     accuracy_equality, demographic_parity, disparate_impact_ratio, equal_opportunity, equalized_odds, predictive_parity
german_credit_lending    age              0/6     -
healthcare_readmission   age              3/6     accuracy_equality, demographic_parity, disparate_impact_ratio
healthcare_readmission   gender           3/6     accuracy_equality, demographic_parity, disparate_impact_ratio
healthcare_readmission   race             1/6     accuracy_equality
insurance_denial         age              0/6     -
insurance_denial         gender           0/6     -
tenant_screening         race             4/6     demographic_parity, disparate_impact_ratio, equal_opportunity, equalized_odds

9 of 13 audit/attribute pairs have some metrics significant and others not.
```

They mostly do not agree. COMPAS fails all six. German Credit and Insurance Denial fail none. The other 9 of 13 pairs fail some and pass others: Benefits Denial by sex fails demographic parity, disparate impact, accuracy equality and predictive parity but not equal opportunity or equalized odds, while Tenant Screening by race is the reverse for predictive parity and accuracy equality. The same model, the same audit, and the verdict depends on the metric.

Three worked paths from the repo's audits:

- **Tenant Screening (a flag leads to refusal):** the harm is a wrongful flag, so start with the false positive rate and equalized odds, then check demographic parity.
- **Benefits Denial (a means test):** the harm is wrongly excluding eligible people, so start with equal opportunity.
- **COMPAS (a risk score shown to a judge):** the harm is a score that means different things by group, so start with predictive parity and calibration, then accept that error-rate parity cannot also hold when base rates differ.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/choosing-a-fairness-metric.py`; that file is generated from the block below). It reads the benchmark's current results; change `strategy` or `model` to look at another.

```python
import pandas as pd

results = pd.read_csv("results/results_fairness.csv")      # the benchmark's current results
base = results[(results.strategy == "unawareness_proxy_removal") & (results.model == "logistic_regression")
               & ~results.protected_attribute.str.contains("_x_")]
rows = []
for (audit, attribute), group in base.groupby(["audit", "protected_attribute"]):
    flagged = sorted(group[group.significant == True].metric)    # noqa: E712 - a boolean column
    rows.append((audit, attribute, len(flagged), len(group), ", ".join(m.replace("_diff", "") for m in flagged)))

print(f"{'audit':24s} {'attribute':16s} flagged  which metrics are significant")
for audit, attribute, n_flagged, n_total, which in rows:
    print(f"{audit:24s} {attribute:16s} {n_flagged}/{n_total}     {which or '-'}")

split = [r for r in rows if 0 < r[2] < r[3]]
print(f"\n{len(split)} of {len(rows)} audit/attribute pairs have some metrics significant and others not.")
```

## Limitations

1. **"Significant" depends on sample size.** A metric can look fine because the group is small, see [Permutation Tests for Fairness Gaps](permutation-test-fairness-gaps.md).
2. **The table assumes the label is right.** If the label is biased, every error-rate row inherits it.
3. **One metric is rarely enough.** Reporting the chosen metric plus the ones that disagree is more honest than reporting one.
4. **Legal standards decide some choices.** Where a regulator names a metric, the choice is made for you.
5. **The conflicts are mathematical.** When base rates differ, no model can satisfy calibration and equal error rates together, see [Fairness Metric Conflicts](fairness-metric-conflicts.md).

## Related Concepts

* [Fairness Metric Conflicts](fairness-metric-conflicts.md) - why you must choose
* [Demographic Parity](demographic-parity.md), [Equal Opportunity](equal-opportunity.md), [Equalized Odds](equalized-odds.md) - the main candidates
* [Predictive Parity](predictive-parity.md) and [Calibration](calibration.md) - the score-meaning family
* [Max-Min (Rawlsian) Fairness](maxmin-fairness.md) - a different kind of answer
* [Disaggregated Evaluation](disaggregated-evaluation.md) - look at the per-group numbers before choosing

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`results/`](../results/) - the benchmark rows used above
* [Benchmark Results Dashboard](../benchmark.html) - filter the same table interactively

## Further Reading

* [Chouldechova, A. (2017): Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.07524) - Big Data 5(2); why equal error rates and equal predictive value conflict when base rates differ.
* [Kleinberg, J., Mullainathan, S., Raghavan, M. (2016): Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.05807) - ITCS 2017; the impossibility result for calibration and balance.
* [Verma, S., Rubin, J. (2018): Fairness Definitions Explained](https://fairware.cs.umass.edu/papers/Verma.pdf) - FairWare 2018; a catalogue of the definitions with a worked example for each.

# Model Cards
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/model-cards.html
Summary: Learn what belongs on a model card: intended use, data, per-group performance and known limits. See one generated from the benchmark's results for Benefits Denial, with every number read straight from results/, and what a card cannot promise.

> *A model card does not make a model fair. It makes it possible to see, before anyone relies on it, who it was built for and who it fails.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

A **model card** is a short, standard document that states what a model is for, what data it was trained on, how it performs overall and for each group, and where it should not be used.

## Why It Matters

A fairness audit produces numbers, and numbers that live in a notebook do not reach the person deciding whether to deploy. A model card is the container that carries them: the same headings every time, so a reader can compare two models, and an explicit place for the uncomfortable results.

It also changes what gets measured. If the card has a per-group table, someone has to fill it in, and an empty row is visible. The card is a disclosure, not a guarantee, and a card that is only a list of reassurances is worse than none.

## Core Concept: Fixed Headings, Per-Group Numbers

The usual sections, from Mitchell and colleagues (2019):

1. **Model details:** what it is, who built it, which version.
2. **Intended use:** the tasks it is for, and the ones it is explicitly not for.
3. **Factors:** the groups and conditions performance was reported across.
4. **Metrics:** what was measured and why.
5. **Evaluation and training data:** where they came from and how they were split.
6. **Quantitative analyses:** the results, **disaggregated** by the factors above ([Disaggregated Evaluation](disaggregated-evaluation.md)).
7. **Ethical considerations and caveats:** what is known to be wrong or unmeasured.

The strongest habit is generating the numeric sections from the audit's output instead of typing them, so the card cannot disagree with the results.

## Concrete Example: Benefits Denial

This card is generated, not hand-written: the numbers are read straight from the benchmark's `results/` (the current results) for the S2 logistic regression on [Benefits Denial](../Benefits%20Denial/).

```
# Model card: logistic_regression on benefits_denial (strategy unawareness_proxy_removal)

## Intended use
A benchmark model that predicts whether income is above $50K, framed as a means-test proxy for benefits
eligibility. It is a teaching and audit artefact, not for deciding real applications.

## Training data
UCI Adult Census Income, features: the audit's core columns only (no protected attribute, no proxy columns).

## Overall performance (test split, 95% bootstrap interval)
- accuracy: 0.811 [0.802, 0.820]
- auc: 0.772
- f1: 0.433 [0.406, 0.459]

## Per-group results (gap = disadvantaged minus advantaged)
- age: demographic parity gap +0.028 (significant, n=944 vs 5569), equal opportunity gap +0.013
- national_origin: demographic parity gap +0.005 (not significant, n=688 vs 5825), equal opportunity gap +0.061
- race: demographic parity gap -0.042 (significant, n=690 vs 5823), equal opportunity gap +0.031
- sex: demographic parity gap -0.051 (significant, n=2153 vs 4360), equal opportunity gap +0.018

## Known limits
- Gaps are measured on one test split; see the intervals and p-values in results/results_fairness.csv.
- Groups smaller than 30 test rows carry small_sample_warning in the results file.
```

Everything under "Overall performance" and "Per-group results" is read from the CSV, including the intervals and the significance flags. The narrative sections (intended use, training data, limits) are the part a person has to write, and they matter as much: the first line of "Intended use" says this is an audit artefact, not for real decisions.

What the card shows that the accuracy alone does not: accuracy is 0.811, but sex and race have significant parity gaps (-0.051 and -0.042), the age gap (+0.028) is significant in the other direction, and national origin is not significant at all.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/model-cards.py`; that file is generated from the block below). It reads the benchmark's current results; change the three constants at the top to document another model.

```python
import pandas as pd

AUDIT, STRATEGY, MODEL = "benefits_denial", "unawareness_proxy_removal", "logistic_regression"
fair = pd.read_csv("results/results_fairness.csv")          # the benchmark's current results
perf = pd.read_csv("results/results_performance.csv")
f = fair[(fair.audit == AUDIT) & (fair.strategy == STRATEGY) & (fair.model == MODEL)]
p = perf[(perf.audit == AUDIT) & (perf.strategy == STRATEGY) & (perf.model == MODEL)].set_index("metric")

print(f"# Model card: {MODEL} on {AUDIT} (strategy {STRATEGY})\n")
print("## Intended use\nA benchmark model that predicts whether income is above $50K, framed as a means-test proxy for benefits")
print("eligibility. It is a teaching and audit artefact, not for deciding real applications.\n")
print("## Training data\nUCI Adult Census Income, features: the audit's core columns only (no protected attribute, no proxy columns).\n")
print("## Overall performance (test split, 95% bootstrap interval)")
for metric in ("accuracy", "auc", "f1"):
    r = p.loc[metric]
    ci = "" if pd.isna(r.ci_low) else f" [{r.ci_low:.3f}, {r.ci_high:.3f}]"
    print(f"- {metric}: {r.value:.3f}{ci}")
print("\n## Per-group results (gap = disadvantaged minus advantaged)")
for attribute, g in f[~f.protected_attribute.str.contains("_x_")].groupby("protected_attribute"):
    parity = g[g.metric == "demographic_parity_diff"].iloc[0]
    equal_opp = g[g.metric == "equal_opportunity_diff"].iloc[0]
    flag = "significant" if parity.significant else "not significant"
    print(f"- {attribute}: demographic parity gap {parity.value:+.3f} ({flag}, n={int(parity.n_disadvantaged)} vs {int(parity.n_advantaged)}), "
          f"equal opportunity gap {equal_opp.value:+.3f}")
print("\n## Known limits\n- Gaps are measured on one test split; see the intervals and p-values in results/results_fairness.csv.")
print("- Groups smaller than 30 test rows carry small_sample_warning in the results file.")
```

## Limitations

1. **A card is a disclosure, not a guarantee.** It tells readers what was measured. It does not make the model safe to use.
2. **It is only as good as its evaluation.** A card built on a small or unrepresentative test set looks authoritative and is not. See [Sampling Bias](sampling-bias.md).
3. **It goes stale.** A model retrained on new data, or a population that has shifted ([Model Drift](model-drift.md)), makes the numbers wrong without changing the card.
4. **Missing groups are invisible.** The card reports only the groups someone chose to evaluate. A group nobody measured has no row.
5. **The caveats are the hard part.** Intended use and known limits need judgement that no script can generate.

## Related Concepts

* [Disaggregated Evaluation](disaggregated-evaluation.md) - the per-group tables a card is built around
* [Datasheets for Datasets](datasheets-for-datasets.md) - the matching document for the training data
* [ML Bias](ml-bias.md) - the sources of bias the caveats section should name
* [Accuracy Is Not Enough in Healthcare AI](accuracy-not-enough-healthcare-ai.md) - why a headline number is not a safety claim
* [Model Drift](model-drift.md) - why a card needs a date and a review
* [Algorithmic Impact Assessment](algorithmic-impact-assessment.md) - the review that a model card feeds into

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Benefits Denial/`](../Benefits%20Denial/) - the audit the card describes
* [`results/`](../results/) - where every number on the card comes from

## Further Reading

* [Mitchell, M. et al. (2019): Model Cards for Model Reporting](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993) - FAT* 2019; the proposal and the section list.
* [Raji, I. D. et al. (2020): Closing the AI Accountability Gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00973) - FAT* 2020; where documentation fits in an end-to-end audit.
* [Barocas, S., Hardt, M., Narayanan, A. (2023): Fairness and Machine Learning](https://fairmlbook.org) - MIT Press; on reporting and documenting model behaviour.

# Datasheets for Datasets
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/datasheets-for-datasets.html
Summary: Learn the datasheet questions and how each unanswered one maps to a bias. See a datasheet for the Healthcare Readmission data filled from the file itself: 101,766 rows, 96.9% of weight values missing, and three questions the repo cannot answer.

> *Most dataset problems are not in the data. They are in the questions nobody asked about where it came from.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

A **datasheet for a dataset** is a short list of standard questions, covering why the data was made, what is in it, how it was collected and processed, and what it should and should not be used for, answered in writing so a user can judge whether it fits their purpose.

## Why It Matters

The audits in this repo each start with a CSV downloaded from somewhere, and almost every bias in the explainers can be traced to a gap in what is known about that file: who was sampled ([Sampling Bias](sampling-bias.md)), who is missing ([Missing Data as Bias in EHRs](missing-data-bias-ehr.md)), how the label was produced ([Label Bias](label-bias.md)), which people were filtered out first ([Survivorship Bias](survivorship-bias.md)).

Electronics ship with a datasheet describing what each component can and cannot do. Datasets usually ship with nothing. The proposal by Gebru and colleagues is to answer the same questions every time, so that an unknown is visible as an unknown.

## Core Concept: Five Question Groups

1. **Motivation:** why was it created, by whom, with whose money?
2. **Composition:** what is an instance, how many are there, what is the label, who is in it, what is missing, is anything sensitive?
3. **Collection:** how was it acquired, over what period, did people consent?
4. **Preprocessing:** what was cleaned, filtered or relabelled, and is the raw data kept?
5. **Uses:** what has it been used for, and what should it not be used for?

Half of the composition answers can be computed from the file. The other half cannot, and an honest datasheet says so instead of guessing.

## Concrete Example: Healthcare Readmission

This datasheet is generated for the [Healthcare Readmission](../Healthcare%20Readmission/) audit data (the 130-hospital diabetes dataset). Everything computable is read from the file and the audit manifest; the questions the repo cannot answer are printed as UNKNOWN.

```
Datasheet: Healthcare Readmission - Clinical Bias

MOTIVATION
  Why was the dataset created, by whom, who funded it?    UNKNOWN: not recorded in this repo

COMPOSITION
  Instances in the file                                   101,766 rows, 50 columns
  Instances after the audit's row filters                 99,492 (2 filters)
  Positive rate of the target (readmitted)                11.2%
  Largest groups of gender                                Female 53.8%, Male 46.2%, Unknown/Invalid 0.0%
  Largest groups of race                                  Caucasian 74.8%, AfricanAmerican 18.9%, ? 2.2%, Hispanic 2.0%
  Largest groups of age                                   [70-80) 25.6%, [60-70) 22.1%, [50-60) 17.0%, [80-90) 16.9%
  Missing values in weight                                96.9%
  Missing values in max_glu_serum                         94.7%
  Missing values in A1Cresult                             83.3%
  Does it contain sensitive attributes?                   yes: race, gender, age

COLLECTION
  How was the data acquired, over what period?            UNKNOWN: not recorded in this repo
  Did the people in it consent to this use?               UNKNOWN: not recorded in this repo

USES
  Used for                                                the Healthcare Readmission audit and the benchmark harness
  Should it be used for clinical decisions?               no: one health system, one coding scheme

3 of the questions above cannot be answered from the repo.
```

The computable answers already matter. After the audit's two row filters 99,492 of 101,766 rows remain and the positive rate is 11.2%. Race is 74.8% Caucasian and 18.9% African American, with 2.2% recorded as `?`. The missingness table is the sharper finding: `weight` is missing for 96.9% of rows, `max_glu_serum` for 94.7% and `A1Cresult` for 83.3%, so any model that uses them is learning from the few rows where a test happened to be ordered, which is exactly the pattern [Missing Data as Bias in EHRs](missing-data-bias-ehr.md) describes.

Three questions cannot be answered from the repo: why the data was created, how it was acquired, and whether the patients consented to this use. Those unknowns are part of the dataset's description.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/datasheets-for-datasets.py`; that file is generated from the block below). Change the folder name to produce one for another audit.

```python
import pandas as pd
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit

data = load_audit("Healthcare Readmission")                  # applies the manifest's row filters and target
manifest = data.manifest
raw = pd.read_csv(manifest.dataset_path, low_memory=False)
missing = raw.replace("?", pd.NA).isna().mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
unknown = []

def ask(question, answer=None):
    if answer is None:
        unknown.append(question)
        answer = "UNKNOWN: not recorded in this repo"
    print(f"  {question:55s} {answer}")

print(f"Datasheet: {manifest.title}\n")
print("MOTIVATION")
ask("Why was the dataset created, by whom, who funded it?")
print("\nCOMPOSITION")
ask("Instances in the file", f"{len(raw):,} rows, {raw.shape[1]} columns")
ask("Instances after the audit's row filters", f"{len(data.y):,} ({len(manifest.row_filters)} filters)")
ask(f"Positive rate of the target ({manifest.target.column})", f"{data.y.mean():.1%}")
for pa in manifest.protected_attributes:
    shares = raw[pa.column].value_counts(normalize=True).head(4)
    ask(f"Largest groups of {pa.column}", ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.1%}" for k, v in shares.items()))
for col, share in missing.head(3).items():
    ask(f"Missing values in {col}", f"{share:.1%}")
ask("Does it contain sensitive attributes?", "yes: race, gender, age")
print("\nCOLLECTION")
ask("How was the data acquired, over what period?")
ask("Did the people in it consent to this use?")
print("\nUSES")
ask("Used for", "the Healthcare Readmission audit and the benchmark harness")
ask("Should it be used for clinical decisions?", "no: one health system, one coding scheme")
print(f"\n{len(unknown)} of the questions above cannot be answered from the repo.")
```

## Limitations

1. **It documents; it does not fix.** A datasheet makes a problem visible and leaves the problem in place.
2. **The unanswerable questions need a person.** Motivation, consent and collection come from the data's authors, not from the file.
3. **Computed answers can mislead.** A `?` counted as missing is a convention. The same file coded differently would give a different missingness figure.
4. **Datasheets go stale.** A dataset that is updated or re-filtered needs a new sheet.
5. **It is not a licence to use.** A complete datasheet can say the data is unsuitable, and that is its best outcome.

## Related Concepts

* [Model Cards](model-cards.md) - the matching document for the model trained on the data
* [Sampling Bias](sampling-bias.md) - the composition questions are how you spot it
* [Missing Data as Bias in EHRs](missing-data-bias-ehr.md) - what the missingness numbers above mean
* [Label Bias](label-bias.md) - the collection and preprocessing questions expose it
* [Protected Attribute](protected-attribute.md) - the sensitive columns the composition section must name
* [Algorithmic Impact Assessment](algorithmic-impact-assessment.md) - where a dataset's unknowns enter a deployment review

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Healthcare Readmission/`](../Healthcare%20Readmission/) - the audit data described above
* [Open Dataset Profiler](../profiler.html) - computes the composition answers for any file

## Further Reading

* [Gebru, T. et al. (2021): Datasheets for Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09010) - Communications of the ACM 64(12); the question list and the motivation.
* [Bender, E. M., Friedman, B. (2018): Data Statements for Natural Language Processing](https://aclanthology.org/Q18-1041/) - TACL 6; the same idea for language data.
* [Holland, S. et al. (2018): The Dataset Nutrition Label](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.03677) - a related, more quantitative proposal for summarizing a dataset.

# Algorithmic Impact Assessment
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/algorithmic-impact-assessment.html
Summary: Learn what an impact assessment asks and how a fairness audit is its measurement step. See the measurement section for Tenant Screening written from results/: four of six metrics significant, and the mitigation options with their gaps.

> *An audit tells you how big the gap is. An impact assessment asks who is on the other side of it, and what happens to them.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

An **algorithmic impact assessment** is a structured review, done before an automated decision system is deployed and repeated afterwards, of who the system affects, what can go wrong for them, how that was measured, and what will be done about it.

## Why It Matters

Everything else in this repo is measurement: a gap, an interval, a p-value. A decision to deploy needs more than measurement. It needs a statement of who is affected, what the alternatives are, who can appeal, and who is accountable. Without a structure, the measurement gets handed over as a number and the judgement around it is skipped.

Impact assessments are that structure. Public bodies have used them for automated decisions, and several jurisdictions require some form of one for high-risk systems. The exact obligations differ by place and change quickly, so rely on the primary text for your own jurisdiction instead of a summary.

## Core Concept: The Measurement Is One Section

A typical assessment has parts that no audit script can supply:

1. **Purpose and alternatives:** what decision, why automate it, what was the non-automated process.
2. **Who is affected:** the people the decision touches, including those who never interact with the system.
3. **Measured disparity:** the audit results, with intervals and the metrics chosen and why ([Choosing a Fairness Metric](choosing-a-fairness-metric.md)).
4. **Mitigation:** what was tried and what it cost.
5. **Safeguards:** human review, appeal, notice, logging.
6. **Monitoring:** what is re-measured after deployment and when it triggers a review.

Section 3 is exactly what the benchmark produces, so it can be generated.

## Concrete Example: Tenant Screening

This is the measurement section of an assessment for the [Tenant Screening](../Tenant%20Screening/) audit, generated from the benchmark's `results/` (the current results) for the S2 logistic regression. Sections 1, 2 and 6 are written by a person; the script prints what it can compute and says what it cannot.

```
Impact assessment, measurement section: tenant_screening (logistic_regression, unawareness_proxy_removal)

1. Who is affected: rental applicants, grouped here by race (Black vs White). Intersections: not measured by this audit.
2. Decision: the model flags an applicant as likely to reoffend within three years; a flag leads to refusal in the framing of the audit.

3. Disparity measured on the held-out test split:
   demographic_parity_diff    +0.114  95% CI [+0.088, +0.138]  p=0.000  SIGNIFICANT
   disparate_impact_ratio     +1.186  95% CI [+1.140, +1.232]  p=0.000  SIGNIFICANT
   equal_opportunity_diff     +0.084  95% CI [+0.053, +0.116]  p=0.000  SIGNIFICANT
   equalized_odds_diff        +0.149  95% CI [+0.109, +0.193]  p=0.000  SIGNIFICANT
   predictive_parity_diff     -0.029  95% CI [-0.061, +0.002]  p=0.072  not significant
   accuracy_equality_diff     -0.012  95% CI [-0.039, +0.015]  p=0.399  not significant

4. Finding: 4 of 6 metrics are significant at 0.05: demographic_parity_diff, disparate_impact_ratio, equal_opportunity_diff, equalized_odds_diff.
5. Mitigation options measured by the benchmark (same audit, same model):
   baseline                     demographic parity gap +0.054  p=0.000
   in_processing                demographic parity gap +0.017  p=0.178
   post_processing              demographic parity gap -0.005  p=0.689
   unawareness                  demographic parity gap +0.119  p=0.000
   unawareness_proxy_removal    demographic parity gap +0.114  p=0.000

6. Not measured here, and needed before deployment: who reviews flags, an appeal route, the legal basis for using
   this data, and a repeat of this measurement after deployment.
```

Reading it as an assessor: four of the six metrics are significant, the flagged-rate gap is +0.114 with an interval of +0.088 to +0.138, and the mitigation table shows what the benchmark's strategies leave behind. Both in-processing (+0.017, p = 0.178) and post-processing (-0.005, p = 0.689) get the demographic parity gap to a level the test cannot distinguish from zero; removing the race column and the proxies alone does not (+0.114).

The last paragraph matters most: who reviews a flag, whether there is an appeal, the legal basis for using this data and when the measurement is repeated are not in any results file, and an assessment that leaves them blank has not been completed.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/algorithmic-impact-assessment.py`; that file is generated from the block below). It reads the benchmark's current results; change the three constants at the top to assess another audit.

```python
import pandas as pd

AUDIT, STRATEGY, MODEL = "tenant_screening", "unawareness_proxy_removal", "logistic_regression"
fair = pd.read_csv("results/results_fairness.csv")          # the benchmark's current results
g = fair[(fair.audit == AUDIT) & (fair.strategy == STRATEGY) & (fair.model == MODEL) & (fair.protected_attribute == "race")]

print(f"Impact assessment, measurement section: {AUDIT} ({MODEL}, {STRATEGY})\n")
print("1. Who is affected: rental applicants, grouped here by race (Black vs White). Intersections: not measured by this audit.")
print("2. Decision: the model flags an applicant as likely to reoffend within three years; a flag leads to refusal in the framing of the audit.\n")
print("3. Disparity measured on the held-out test split:")
for r in g.itertuples():
    verdict = "SIGNIFICANT" if r.significant else "not significant"
    print(f"   {r.metric:26s} {r.value:+.3f}  95% CI [{r.ci_low:+.3f}, {r.ci_high:+.3f}]  p={r.p_value:.3f}  {verdict}")
flagged = g[g.significant == True]                                   # noqa: E712 - a boolean column
print(f"\n4. Finding: {len(flagged)} of {len(g)} metrics are significant at 0.05: " + ", ".join(sorted(flagged.metric)) + ".")
print("5. Mitigation options measured by the benchmark (same audit, same model):")
for strategy, rows in fair[(fair.audit == AUDIT) & (fair.model == MODEL) & (fair.protected_attribute == "race")
                           & (fair.metric == "demographic_parity_diff")].groupby("strategy"):
    r = rows.iloc[0]
    print(f"   {strategy:28s} demographic parity gap {r.value:+.3f}  p={r.p_value:.3f}")
print("\n6. Not measured here, and needed before deployment: who reviews flags, an appeal route, the legal basis for using")
print("   this data, and a repeat of this measurement after deployment.")
```

## Limitations

1. **It documents risk; it does not remove it.** A complete assessment can conclude that a system should not be deployed.
2. **Measurement is only one part.** A good fairness number can sit beside an unfair process with no appeal.
3. **The legal landscape moves.** Required content and trigger conditions change, so use the current primary source for your jurisdiction.
4. **It is a snapshot.** Without the monitoring step, the numbers describe the day of the audit, see [Model Drift](model-drift.md).
5. **Affected people are rarely in the room.** An assessment written only by the builders tends to miss harms they would not think of. Involving affected groups is a design choice, not a script.

# Inferring Protected Attributes
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/inferring-protected-attributes.html
Summary: Learn how group membership is estimated from other fields and what that does to a measured gap. See Benefits Denial with sex hidden: inferred from 5% labelled rows at 0.823 accuracy, the gap reads -0.092 (hard) or -0.0885 (weighted) against a true -0.1003.

> *You cannot audit a gap you cannot see. When the group is missing, you estimate it, and the estimate has its own error.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Inferring protected attributes** means estimating each person's group membership from other fields (a surname and address, a name list, a trained classifier) so a fairness gap can be measured when the true attribute was never collected.

## Why It Matters

Many organizations are not allowed to collect race, or never did: lenders in the United States are generally barred from asking about race on most consumer credit applications, and many datasets simply do not have the column. They still need to know whether a model treats groups differently. The usual answer is to estimate the attribute, which is how regulators and lenders have measured disparity in practice.

That swaps one problem for another. The estimate is wrong for some people, and the errors are not random: they follow the same correlations the proxies do. How wrong the measured gap becomes is the question.

## Core Concept: Hard Labels or Probabilities

Given an estimated probability `p` that each person is in the disadvantaged group, there are two ways to compute a group gap in the model's decisions `d`:

```
hard label:           assign each person to their most likely group, then compare group means of d
probability-weighted: gap = sum(p * d) / sum(p)  -  sum((1 - p) * d) / sum(1 - p)
```

The weighted version uses every person's uncertainty instead of rounding it away. Both are biased toward zero when the estimate is noisy, because mislabelled people blur the two groups together. That attenuation is the thing to measure.

## Concrete Example: Benefits Denial

[Benefits Denial](../Benefits%20Denial/): the audited model is logistic regression on the core and proxy columns, with sex removed. We pretend sex was never recorded, train a reader on sex labels for only 5% of the training rows (1,302 rows), and use it to estimate sex for the test rows. The truth is known, so the error of each estimate is visible.

```
true sex available: parity gap -0.1003  (women 0.052, men 0.152)
inferred from 1302 labelled rows: accuracy 0.823, AUC 0.916
most likely group (hard label): parity gap -0.0920
probability-weighted:           parity gap -0.0885
```

With the true sex available the gap is -0.1003 (women flagged 5.2%, men 15.2%), which is the benchmark's S1 row in `results/` (the current results). The reader is decent, with 0.823 accuracy and 0.916 AUC, and the estimates of the gap are:

- **Hard labels:** -0.0920, about 8% smaller in size than the truth.
- **Probability-weighted:** -0.0885, about 12% smaller.

Both point the right way and are the right order of magnitude, and both understate the gap. In this run the hard labels happened to do slightly better than the weighted estimate; that is one dataset and one reader, not a rule.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/inferring-protected-attributes.py`; that file is generated from the block below). The true attribute is used only to score the result.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness
from faircode.models import build_model

data = load_audit("Benefits Denial", strategy="unawareness")   # core + proxy columns, no sex column
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
women = data.masks["sex"].to_numpy()                          # the true group, which we pretend is missing
y = data.y.to_numpy()
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# 1. The audited model (the same S1 model whose gap we want to measure).
audited = build_model("logistic_regression", data.random_state).fit(data.X.iloc[train], y[train])
pred = audited.predict(data.X.iloc[test])
truth = women[test]
true_gap = pred[truth == 1].mean() - pred[truth == 0].mean()
print(f"true sex available: parity gap {true_gap:+.4f}  (women {pred[truth == 1].mean():.3f}, men {pred[truth == 0].mean():.3f})")

# 2. Infer sex from the other columns, using sex labels for only 5% of the TRAINING rows.
labelled = rng.choice(train, size=int(0.05 * len(train)), replace=False)
reader = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=data.random_state, n_jobs=-1)
reader.fit(data.X.iloc[labelled], women[labelled])
p_woman = reader.predict_proba(data.X.iloc[test])[:, 1]
print(f"inferred from {len(labelled)} labelled rows: accuracy {((p_woman >= 0.5) == truth).mean():.3f}, AUC {roc_auc_score(truth, p_woman):.3f}")

# 3. Two ways to use the inferred group to estimate the gap.
hard = p_woman >= 0.5
hard_gap = pred[hard].mean() - pred[~hard].mean()
soft_gap = (p_woman * pred).sum() / p_woman.sum() - ((1 - p_woman) * pred).sum() / (1 - p_woman).sum()
print(f"most likely group (hard label): parity gap {hard_gap:+.4f}")
print(f"probability-weighted:           parity gap {soft_gap:+.4f}")
```

## Limitations

1. **The estimate understates the gap.** Misclassification blurs the groups, so the measured gap is usually smaller than the true one. Treat it as a lower bound unless corrected.
2. **Errors are not random.** The reader is wrong in structured ways, often for the same people the model is wrong for, which can bias the estimate in either direction.
3. **It needs some labels, or a trustworthy external source.** Here 5% of rows had the attribute. With none, you rely on a name list or a census join, which carry their own error rates.
4. **Inferring a protected attribute is itself sensitive.** It creates a record that did not exist. Check what law and policy allow, and keep the inferred column out of the decision system.
5. **Do not use the inferred attribute in the model.** It is a measurement tool for the audit, not an input, see [Fairness Through Unawareness](fairness-through-unawareness.md).

## Related Concepts

* [Protected Attribute](protected-attribute.md) - what is being estimated
* [Proxy Variables](proxy-variables.md) - the same correlations the estimate relies on
* [Fairness Through Unawareness](fairness-through-unawareness.md) - why not having the attribute does not make a model fair
* [Fairness Without Demographics](fairness-without-demographics.md) - improving the model when you cannot measure the groups at all
* [Measurement Bias](measurement-bias.md) - how an error in measuring a group blurs a gap

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Benefits Denial/`](../Benefits%20Denial/) - the audit used for the example above
* [`results/`](../results/) - the benchmark row quoted for S1

## Further Reading

* Elliott, M. N. et al. (2009). Using the Census Bureau's Surname List to Improve Estimates of Race/Ethnicity and Associated Disparities. Health Services and Outcomes Research Methodology 9(2) - the method behind Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding.
* [Chen, J., Kallus, N., Mao, X., Svacha, G., Udell, M. (2019): Fairness Under Unawareness: Assessing Disparity When Protected Class Is Unobserved](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.11154) - FAT* 2019; when a proxy-based estimate of disparity is and is not reliable.
* [Kallus, N., Mao, X., Zhou, A. (2022): Assessing Algorithmic Fairness with Unobserved Protected Class Using Data Combination](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00285) - Management Science; bounds on disparity when the attribute and the outcome sit in different datasets.

# Fairness Without Demographics
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/fairness-without-demographics.html
Summary: Learn how upweighting the training rows a model gets wrong improves worst-group accuracy without any group labels. See it on Benefits Denial: a 3x upweight lifts the worst group from 0.712 to 0.742, and a 5x upweight collapses the model.

> *If you do not know who the worst-off group is, you can still train against the people the model is already getting wrong.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

**Fairness without demographics** is a family of training methods that improve the accuracy of the worst-off groups without ever using group labels, usually by putting more weight on the examples the model finds hardest.

## Why It Matters

[Distributionally Robust Optimization](distributionally-robust-optimization.md) and [Max-Min (Rawlsian) Fairness](maxmin-fairness.md) both need group labels during training, which many teams do not have, are not allowed to use, or do not trust. They also only protect the groups you thought to define.

The label-free idea is that groups a model fails are usually groups with high loss, so high loss stands in for membership. Hashimoto and colleagues showed a worst-case objective can be optimized without labels, and Liu and colleagues made it practical with a two-step recipe: train once, find the rows it got wrong, train again with those rows weighted up.

## Core Concept: Upweight the Errors

```
1. train a first model
2. find the training rows it misclassifies
3. train a second model, giving those rows a weight greater than 1
```

No group appears anywhere. Group labels are used only afterwards, to *evaluate* whether the worst group improved. The weight is the dial: a modest value shifts attention toward hard rows, a large one makes the model chase noise and the rare errors of a class, and the model degrades.

## Concrete Example: Benefits Denial

[Benefits Denial](../Benefits%20Denial/): logistic regression on the core columns, the benchmark's split. The four evaluation groups are sex crossed with age 55 and over, and they are used only to report results.

```
baseline                           overall 0.811 | male <55 0.776 male 55+ 0.712 female <55 0.900 female 55+ 0.901 | worst group 0.712
upweight the errors x1.5           overall 0.811 | male <55 0.778 male 55+ 0.717 female <55 0.898 female 55+ 0.891 | worst group 0.717
upweight the errors x2             overall 0.815 | male <55 0.789 male 55+ 0.725 female <55 0.889 female 55+ 0.874 | worst group 0.725
upweight the errors x3             overall 0.773 | male <55 0.765 male 55+ 0.742 female <55 0.792 female 55+ 0.816 | worst group 0.742
upweight the errors x5             overall 0.607 | male <55 0.626 male 55+ 0.702 female <55 0.526 female 55+ 0.670 | worst group 0.526
```

The baseline is the benchmark's S2 row in `results/` (the current results): 0.811 accuracy, with the worst group, men 55 and over, at 0.712.

- **A small upweight helps.** At 2x the worst group improves to 0.725 and overall accuracy to 0.815.
- **A larger one helps the worst group more and costs the rest.** At 3x the worst group is at 0.742, but overall accuracy is down to 0.773 and women under 55 drop from 0.900 to 0.792.
- **Past that it breaks.** At 5x the model collapses to 0.607 overall and the worst group, now women under 55, to 0.526.

The "worst group" can change identity: at 5x it is a different group from the baseline's. A label-free method has no way to prefer one group's accuracy over another's; it moves all of them.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/fairness-without-demographics.py`; that file is generated from the block below). Group labels appear only in the evaluation lines.

```python
import numpy as np
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness
from faircode.models import build_model

data = load_audit("Benefits Denial")             # S2 feature set: core features, no protected columns
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
X, y = data.X, data.y.to_numpy()
sex, aged = data.masks["sex"].to_numpy(), data.masks["age"].to_numpy()
group = sex * 2 + aged                           # used ONLY to evaluate, never to train
labels = ["male <55", "male 55+", "female <55", "female 55+"]

def fit(weights=None):
    return build_model("logistic_regression", data.random_state).fit(X.iloc[train], y[train], sample_weight=weights)

def report(name, model):
    correct = model.predict(X.iloc[test]) == y[test]
    per_group = [correct[group[test] == k].mean() for k in range(4)]
    print(f"{name:34s} overall {correct.mean():.3f} | " + " ".join(f"{l} {a:.3f}" for l, a in zip(labels, per_group))
          + f" | worst group {min(per_group):.3f}")

baseline = fit()
report("baseline", baseline)

# Just Train Twice: upweight the training rows the first model got wrong. No group labels are used.
wrong = baseline.predict(X.iloc[train]) != y[train]
for upweight in (1.5, 2, 3, 5):
    report(f"upweight the errors x{upweight}", fit(np.where(wrong, upweight, 1.0)))
```

## Limitations

1. **The weight is a free parameter, and the cliff is steep.** 2x helped, 3x traded accuracy for the worst group, 5x broke the model. Choose it on held-out data with group labels, which defeats part of the point.
2. **You still need labels to know it worked.** The method trains without them, but evaluation needs them, see [Disaggregated Evaluation](disaggregated-evaluation.md).
3. **High loss is not the same as a protected group.** The rows a model gets wrong may be label noise or outliers, which upweighting amplifies. See [Label Bias](label-bias.md).
4. **It cannot target a legal standard.** Nothing in it aims at demographic parity or equalized odds.
5. **The gains are modest.** Here the best worst-group change was 3 points, at a cost elsewhere. A method with labels, like [Distributionally Robust Optimization](distributionally-robust-optimization.md), can do more when labels are available.

## Related Concepts

* [Distributionally Robust Optimization](distributionally-robust-optimization.md) - the worst-group objective that needs labels
* [Max-Min (Rawlsian) Fairness](maxmin-fairness.md) - the hard-error version, also needing labels
* [Inferring Protected Attributes](inferring-protected-attributes.md) - estimating the groups instead of avoiding them
* [Class Imbalance](class-imbalance.md) - the same weighting mechanics
* [Disaggregated Evaluation](disaggregated-evaluation.md) - how to check the worst group afterwards

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Benefits Denial/`](../Benefits%20Denial/) - the audit used for the example above
* [`results/`](../results/) - the benchmark row quoted for S2

## Further Reading

* [Hashimoto, T., Srivastava, M., Namkoong, H., Liang, P. (2018): Fairness Without Demographics in Repeated Loss Minimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.08010) - ICML 2018; a worst-case objective optimized without group labels.
* [Liu, E. Z. et al. (2021): Just Train Twice: Improving Group Robustness without Training Group Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.09044) - ICML 2021; the two-step upweighting recipe used above.
* [Lahoti, P. et al. (2020): Fairness without Demographics through Adversarially Reweighted Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.13114) - NeurIPS 2020; learns the weights with an adversary instead of fixing them.

# Adverse Action Notices
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/adverse-action-notices.html
Summary: Learn what an adverse action notice and its reason codes are, and how to derive them from a model's contributions. See German Credit Lending: the top reason is identical for both age groups, but personal_status appears 15 points more often in the under-30s' top two reasons.

> *A decline is not an explanation. The reasons a lender must give are the one place a model's inputs are forced into the open, and they can show a proxy the audit missed.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

An **adverse action notice** is the notice a lender must give an applicant who is declined or offered worse terms, and the **reason codes** on it are the specific main factors in the model's score that led to the decision.

## Why It Matters

In the United States the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and its Regulation B (12 CFR 1002.9) require a creditor to tell a declined applicant the specific principal reasons, or how to ask for them, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has said that using a complex algorithm is not an excuse for a vague reason. Check the current text and your jurisdiction before relying on any summary here, including this one.

Reason codes matter for fairness for a second reason. A model has a coefficient for every input, but nobody reads a coefficient table. A reason code is the same information turned into a sentence an applicant and a regulator will read, so a reason like "marital status" or "neighbourhood" stops being a column name and becomes a statement that a protected characteristic influenced the decision.

## Core Concept: Contributions Relative to the Average Applicant

For a linear model, each feature's contribution to an applicant's log-odds is its coefficient times how far the applicant's standardized value is from the average. The reasons are the features with the most negative contributions, in order. For a non-linear model the same idea is carried by Shapley values ([SHAP Values](shap-values.md)).

```
contribution_j  =  coefficient_j * (standardized value_j)      relative to the average applicant
reason codes    =  the 2 to 4 features with the most negative contribution
```

Two properties to keep in mind. The reasons are relative to a reference applicant, which is a choice. And the reasons explain the score, not the world: they say what moved the model, not what the applicant could change ([Algorithmic Recourse](algorithmic-recourse.md)).

## Concrete Example: German Credit Lending

[German Credit Lending](../German%20Credit%20Lending/): logistic regression on the audit's core features with age left out, standardized. The model declines 185 of the 1,000 applicants (the model is fitted on the benchmark's training rows and applied to every row, to get enough declines to count). The main reason for each is its most negative contribution.

```
the model declines 185 of 1000 applicants

age 30 and over: 97 declined (15% of the group); main reason
  checking_status          62%
  credit_amount            18%
  duration                 9%
  personal_status          6%

under 30: 88 declined (24% of the group); main reason
  checking_status          62%
  credit_amount            12%
  personal_status          12%
  purpose                  9%

largest differences in how often a reason is in an applicant's top two (under 30 minus 30 and over):
reason
personal_status    0.15
purpose           -0.06
duration          -0.05
```

Two things stand out. The headline reason is the same for both age groups (`checking_status`, 62% each), so a quick look at the top reason would find nothing. But the second layer differs: `personal_status` is the main reason for 12% of the under-30s declined against 6% of the others, and across an applicant's top two reasons it appears 15 points more often for the under-30s. In this dataset `personal_status` is the Statlog attribute that combines sex and marital status, so for a real lender a reason code of that kind would be a red flag in itself.

The age gap in declines is also visible: 24% of under-30s are declined against 15% of the rest. The benchmark's S2 row for this audit in `results/` (the current results) gives the same direction, a parity gap of -0.0914, but with a 95% interval of -0.218 to +0.041 and a p-value of 0.17, because the test set is only 200 rows.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/adverse-action-notices.py`; that file is generated from the block below).

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness

data = load_audit("German Credit Lending")       # S2 feature set: core features, no protected column
train = data.idx_train
X = data.X.to_numpy(dtype=float)
Z = (X - X[train].mean(axis=0)) / (X[train].std(axis=0) + 1e-9)
y = data.y.to_numpy()                            # 1 = good credit
young = data.masks["age"].to_numpy().astype(int) # 1 = applicants under 30, the disadvantaged group
columns = np.array(data.X.columns)

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(Z[train], y[train])
declined = np.flatnonzero(model.predict(Z) == 0)  # every applicant the model would decline (all 1,000 rows)

# Reason codes: the features that pushed each declined applicant's score down the most.
contribution = Z[declined] * model.coef_[0]       # per-feature contribution to the log-odds, relative to the average applicant
order = np.argsort(contribution, axis=1)          # most negative first
main_reason = columns[order[:, 0]]

print(f"the model declines {len(declined)} of {len(y)} applicants")
for g, name in ((0, "age 30 and over"), (1, "under 30")):
    rows = young[declined] == g
    shares = pd.Series(main_reason[rows]).value_counts(normalize=True).head(4)
    print(f"\n{name}: {rows.sum()} declined ({rows.sum() / (young == g).sum():.0%} of the group); main reason")
    for reason, share in shares.items():
        print(f"  {reason:24s} {share:.0%}")

top_two = pd.DataFrame({"reason": np.concatenate([columns[order[:, 0]], columns[order[:, 1]]]),
                        "young": np.concatenate([young[declined], young[declined]])})
share = top_two.groupby(["reason", "young"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
share = share / share.sum()
print("\nlargest differences in how often a reason is in an applicant's top two (under 30 minus 30 and over):")
print((share[1] - share[0]).sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False).head(3).round(2).to_string())
```

## Limitations

1. **The reasons depend on the reference applicant.** Relative to the average applicant, relative to the approval threshold, or relative to a typical approved applicant gives different lists. A notice has to say which, and the regulator's expectations on this are for the primary text to settle.
2. **Correlated features split the blame.** Two features that carry the same signal share a contribution, so each may fall below the cut-off for being a "main reason" while together they decided the outcome.
3. **A reason is not a remedy.** "Checking status" tells the applicant what moved the score, not what to change. See [Algorithmic Recourse](algorithmic-recourse.md).
4. **A clean top reason can hide the problem.** Here the first reason was identical across groups, and the difference sat in the second.
5. **Counts are small.** There are 97 and 88 declined applicants in the two groups; the 15-point difference in top-two share is a flag to investigate, not a tested effect. See [Permutation Tests for Fairness Gaps](permutation-test-fairness-gaps.md).

## Related Concepts

* [SHAP Values](shap-values.md) - contributions for models that are not linear
* [Counterfactual Explanation](counterfactual-explanation.md) - the basis for notices that say what would change the decision
* [Algorithmic Recourse](algorithmic-recourse.md) - reasons the applicant can act on
* [Proxy Variables](proxy-variables.md) - why a reason like marital status is a warning
* [Disparate Impact](disparate-impact.md) - the legal test that a pattern in reasons feeds

## Further Reading

* Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (2022). Consumer Financial Protection Circular 2022-03: Adverse action notification requirements in connection with credit decisions based on complex algorithms - what the regulator said about algorithms and specific reasons.
* [Lundberg, S., Lee, S.-I. (2017): A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874) - NeurIPS 2017; Shapley contributions for models beyond linear ones.
* Bracke, P., Datta, A., Jung, C., Sen, S. (2019). Machine Learning Explainability in Finance: An Application to Default Risk Analysis. Bank of England Staff Working Paper 816 - reason-style explanations for a credit model.

# Geographic Proxies and Redlining
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/geographic-proxies-and-redlining.html
Summary: Learn how a location column reconstructs race and how to measure both the proxy and its effect on the gap. See Tenant Screening: the area alone recovers race at 0.719 AUC, yet adding it moves the parity gap from +0.1136 to +0.0812.

> *Where a person lives is the oldest proxy for who they are. A model never has to see race to be told it.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

A **geographic proxy** is a location feature (zip code, census area, neighbourhood) that is correlated enough with a protected attribute that a model using it can reconstruct the attribute, and **redlining** is the historical practice of denying services in areas defined largely by who lived there.

## Why It Matters

In the 1930s federal agencies drew maps grading neighbourhoods by risk, and lenders used them to deny mortgages in the areas graded lowest, which were largely Black neighbourhoods. The maps are gone, but residential segregation is not, so an address still carries information about race. Rothstein's *The Color of Law* traces the history, and later work has measured how the old grades line up with present-day neighbourhood outcomes.

For a modern model the consequence is mechanical. A location feature is cheap to collect, predictive of many outcomes and rarely thought of as sensitive, and it is exactly the kind of column [Proxy Variables](proxy-variables.md) warns about. Whether it moves a fairness gap in practice is an empirical question, and the example below shows it can go either way.

## Core Concept: Two Questions About a Location Column

1. **How much of the attribute does it reveal?** Predict the protected attribute from the location alone, on held-out rows. An AUC well above 0.5 means the location is a proxy. Compare with the model's other features to see whether it is the main route.
2. **What does it do to the gap?** Train the decision model with and without the location and compare the parity gap and accuracy. A strong proxy does not guarantee a wider gap: the location may also carry legitimate signal, and its net effect on decisions can go either way.

## Concrete Example: Tenant Screening

[Tenant Screening](../Tenant%20Screening/) has `Residence_PUMA`, a Census public-use microdata area, for each person. It is not one of the audit's features. The group is Black applicants, the model is logistic regression on the core features, and the split is the benchmark's.

```
25 areas, share of Black residents by area runs from 0.15 to 0.89
race recovered from the area alone: AUC 0.719 (0.5 is chance)
race recovered from the model's own features: AUC 0.655
core features                      accuracy 0.639 | parity gap +0.1136
core features + area               accuracy 0.639 | parity gap +0.0812
```

The 25 areas run from 15% to 89% Black among the people in them. A score that is only the training-set Black share of the person's area recovers race with an AUC of 0.719, better than the model's own features do (0.655). So the area is a strong proxy.

Then the surprise: adding the area as one-hot columns to the recidivism model leaves accuracy unchanged at 0.639 and moves the parity gap from +0.1136 to +0.0812. The proxy is strong and the gap went down. The area carries information about recidivism that the core features were encoding through other, race-correlated columns, and giving the model the area directly changed which columns it leaned on. The lesson is not that location is safe. It is that you cannot read the effect of a proxy from how strong it is, so you have to measure both.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/geographic-proxies-and-redlining.py`; that file is generated from the block below). `data.df` holds the raw rows, so a column the harness does not encode (the area) can still be read.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness

data = load_audit("Tenant Screening")            # S2 feature set: core features, no race, no proxies
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
black = data.masks["race"].to_numpy().astype(int)
area = data.df["Residence_PUMA"].to_numpy()      # a Census public-use microdata area: a neighbourhood-sized region
y = data.y.to_numpy()

# 1. How much of race does the area alone reveal? Use each area's Black share in the training rows as the score.
share = pd.Series(black[train]).groupby(area[train]).mean()
score = pd.Series(area[test]).map(share).fillna(black[train].mean()).to_numpy()
print(f"{len(share)} areas, share of Black residents by area runs from {share.min():.2f} to {share.max():.2f}")
print(f"race recovered from the area alone: AUC {roc_auc_score(black[test], score):.3f} (0.5 is chance)")
core = data.X.to_numpy(dtype=float)
core = (core - core[train].mean(axis=0)) / (core[train].std(axis=0) + 1e-9)
reader = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(core[train], black[train])
print(f"race recovered from the model's own features: AUC {roc_auc_score(black[test], reader.predict_proba(core[test])[:, 1]):.3f}")

# 2. What does adding the area do to a recidivism model's parity gap?
dummies = pd.get_dummies(pd.Series(area), prefix="area").to_numpy(dtype=float)
def report(name, features):
    model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(features[train], y[train])
    pred = model.predict(features[test])
    gap = pred[black[test] == 1].mean() - pred[black[test] == 0].mean()
    print(f"{name:34s} accuracy {(pred == y[test]).mean():.3f} | parity gap {gap:+.4f}")
report("core features", core)
report("core features + area", np.hstack([core, dummies]))
```

## Limitations

1. **A strong proxy is not a verdict.** The gap fell when the area was added. Treat the AUC and the gap change as two separate measurements.
2. **Area resolution matters.** A PUMA is large; zip codes and census blocks are finer and reveal more, and a coarse region reveals less.
3. **Target encoding on the training rows can overfit.** The area-share score here is fitted on the training rows and tested on held-out rows, which is the safe way round. Doing it on all rows inflates the AUC.
4. **It does not show cause.** Residential segregation, policing patterns and economic differences all feed the correlation, and the model cannot tell them apart.
5. **Dropping the location is not automatically fair.** Removing it may push the model onto other proxies, as [Fairness Through Unawareness](fairness-through-unawareness.md) shows.

## Related Concepts

* [Proxy Variables](proxy-variables.md) - the general mechanism, and a chi-squared check for a categorical proxy
* [Proxy Entanglement](proxy-entanglement.md) - when several proxies reinforce each other
* [Fairness Through Unawareness](fairness-through-unawareness.md) - why dropping the column may not help
* [Disparate Treatment](disparate-treatment.md) - when using a location is a direct, intended use
* [Inferring Protected Attributes](inferring-protected-attributes.md) - the same idea used for measurement, not for decisions

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`Tenant Screening/`](../Tenant%20Screening/) - the audit used for the example above

## Further Reading

* Rothstein, R. (2017). *The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America.* Liveright - the history of housing segregation policy.
* Aaronson, D., Hartley, D., Mazumder, B. (2021). The Effects of the 1930s HOLC "Redlining" Maps. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 13(4) - measures the lasting effects of the maps.
* [Barocas, S., Selbst, A. D. (2016): Big Data's Disparate Impact](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2477899) - California Law Review 104; how data mining can reproduce discrimination through proxies.

# Risk-Based Pricing Gaps
URL: https://www.thefaircode.xyz/explainers/risk-based-pricing-gaps.html
Summary: Learn how to measure a fairness gap in a continuous quoted amount or rate when no one is declined. See German Credit Lending: models quote 7 to 13 percent less to under-30s, with intervals that still include zero at 200 test rows.

> *A model can approve everyone and still treat groups differently, by deciding how much to offer or how much to charge. Fairness metrics for yes-or-no decisions do not see it.*

## The One-Sentence Definition

A **pricing gap** is a difference between groups in the amount, rate or term a model quotes to applicants who were all approved, and it is measured as a difference in a continuous outcome instead of a difference in selection rates.

## Why It Matters

Every metric in this repo's benchmark is built on a decision that is yes or no: [Demographic Parity](demographic-parity.md), [Equalized Odds](equalized-odds.md), [Disparate Impact](disparate-impact.md). A lender that approves every applicant passes all of them. It can still offer a smaller line of credit, a higher rate or a shorter term to one group, and that is a decision with the same consequences.

The measurement is simpler than it sounds. The quantity is a number, so the gap is a difference of means, and the uncertainty is a bootstrap interval ([Bootstrap Confidence Intervals](bootstrap-confidence-intervals.md)). The hard parts are choosing the quantity and remembering that the same gap can be fair or unfair depending on whether the difference in price tracks a real difference in risk.

## Core Concept: A Regression, Then a Gap in Its Output

```
1. train a regression for the quoted amount (rate, limit, term) on the non-protected features
2. predict it for the test applicants
3. gap = mean(quoted | disadvantaged) - mean(quoted | advantaged), with a bootstrap interval
4. compare it with the gap in the amounts people actually received, and with the approve or deny gap
```

If the quoted gap is larger than the real-world gap, the model has widened a difference. If it is zero while the approval gap is not, price is not where the unfairness sits.

## Concrete Example: German Credit Lending

[German Credit Lending](../German%20Credit%20Lending/) has a continuous `credit_amount`, which stands in for the amount a lender would offer. Everyone is treated as approved; the model predicts the amount from every other core column, with age left out, using the benchmark's split (200 test applicants, 69 of them under 30).

```
real amounts: under 30 3,277, 30 and over 3,790 (gap -513)
linear regression  quoted amount, under 30 minus 30 and over: -233 (-7%), 95% interval [-802, +308]
gradient boosting  quoted amount, under 30 minus 30 and over: -477 (-13%), 95% interval [-1,039, +94]
```

In the data, under-30s received 513 less on average (3,277 against 3,790). Both models quote a smaller amount to the under-30s too: 233 less (7%) from the linear regression and 477 less (13%) from gradient boosting. The intervals say how much to read into that: [-802, +308] and [-1,039, +94] both include zero. With 200 test rows the data cannot separate a real 13% gap from noise, which is the situation [Permutation Tests for Fairness Gaps](permutation-test-fairness-gaps.md) describes.

For comparison, the same audit's approve-or-deny parity gap in `results/` (the current results, S2 strategy) is -0.0914 with an interval of -0.218 to +0.041. Both are the same direction and both are inconclusive on this sample, and neither alone would show the other.

## Detection/Implementation Code

Run from the repo root (`PYTHONPATH=. python3 explainers/code/risk-based-pricing-gaps.py`; that file is generated from the block below).

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from faircode.benchmark import load_audit        # same loader, encoding and split as the benchmark harness

data = load_audit("German Credit Lending")       # S2 feature set: core features, no protected column
train, test = data.idx_train, data.idx_test
young = data.masks["age"].to_numpy().astype(int)[test]     # 1 = under 30, the disadvantaged group
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Everyone is "approved"; the model decides how much to lend. The quoted amount is predicted from the other
# columns (the one continuous amount a lender sets per applicant in this file).
X = data.X.drop(columns=["credit_amount"])
amount = data.df["credit_amount"].to_numpy(dtype=float)

def bootstrap_gap(values, group, n=2000):
    a, b = values[group == 1], values[group == 0]
    gaps = [rng.choice(a, len(a)).mean() - rng.choice(b, len(b)).mean() for _ in range(n)]
    return np.percentile(gaps, [2.5, 97.5])

print(f"real amounts: under 30 {amount[test][young == 1].mean():,.0f}, 30 and over {amount[test][young == 0].mean():,.0f} "
      f"(gap {amount[test][young == 1].mean() - amount[test][young == 0].mean():+,.0f})")
for name, model in (("linear regression", LinearRegression()),
                    ("gradient boosting", GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=data.random_state))):
    quoted = model.fit(X.iloc[train], amount[train]).predict(X.iloc[test])
    gap = quoted[young == 1].mean() - quoted[young == 0].mean()
    lo, hi = bootstrap_gap(quoted, young)
    relative = gap / quoted[young == 0].mean()
    print(f"{name:18s} quoted amount, under 30 minus 30 and over: {gap:+,.0f} ({relative:+.0%}), 95% interval [{lo:+,.0f}, {hi:+,.0f}]")
```

## Limitations

1. **A price gap is not automatically unfair.** If the quoted amount tracks real differences in risk or need, a gap can be justified. The test is whether the group still gets a worse offer at the same risk, which needs a risk estimate that is itself not biased.
2. **The stand-in outcome is imperfect.** `credit_amount` here is what applicants asked for and received, not an offer. Real pricing data would have the rate and term the lender set.
3. **Small samples hide the answer.** Both intervals cross zero. See [Disaggregated Evaluation](disaggregated-evaluation.md) for how fast intervals widen.
4. **One number per group loses the spread.** A mean gap can hide a gap that only exists at the top or bottom of the distribution, so quantiles or a full comparison of distributions may be needed.
5. **There is no standard threshold.** The four-fifths rule is for selection rates. For prices, the standard is a legal and policy question to answer for your setting, from primary sources.

## Related Concepts

* [Demographic Parity](demographic-parity.md) - the yes-or-no counterpart this extends
* [Disparate Impact](disparate-impact.md) - the legal test, written for selection
* [Bootstrap Confidence Intervals](bootstrap-confidence-intervals.md) - the interval on a difference of means
* [Fairness in Ranking](fairness-in-ranking.md) - another outcome that is not a single decision
* [Adverse Action Notices](adverse-action-notices.md) - what a lender owes an applicant who gets worse terms

## Related Projects in This Repo

* [`German Credit Lending/`](../German%20Credit%20Lending/) - the audit used for the example above
* [`results/`](../results/) - the benchmark row quoted for the approve-or-deny gap

## Further Reading

* [Bartlett, R., Morse, A., Stanton, R., Wallace, N. (2022): Consumer-Lending Discrimination in the FinTech Era](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2021.05.047) - Journal of Financial Economics 143(1); price differences by group in algorithmic and face-to-face mortgage lending.
* [Fuster, A., Goldsmith-Pinkham, P., Ramadorai, T., Walther, A. (2022): Predictably Unequal? The Effects of Machine Learning on Credit Markets](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.13090) - The Journal of Finance 77(1); who gains and loses when lenders move to machine-learning pricing.
* [Barocas, S., Hardt, M., Narayanan, A. (2023): Fairness and Machine Learning](https://fairmlbook.org) - MIT Press; on fairness criteria beyond classification.
